Big idea: the sinuses help warm and moisten the air we breathe, make the skull lighter, and give our voices resonance.

questions.prompt: Gas exchange takes place in the:

choices.explanation: Correct. Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli.
Incorrect. Bronchi are large tubes that only carry air.
Incorrect. Most bronchioles only carry air; gas exchange happens farther down in the alveoli.
Incorrect. The nasal cavity warms, moistens, and filters air but does not exchange gases.
Incorrect. The pharynx is a passageway for air and food.
Incorrect. The trachea is a tube that carries air to the lungs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the alveoli. Alveoli are tiny air sacs at the very end of the airways. Their walls are only one cell thick and are surrounded by a net of capillaries.

Oxygen moves from the air in the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the alveoli, by diffusion. The bronchi, bronchioles, nasal cavity, pharynx, and trachea are all tubes that carry air to the alveoli; their walls are too thick for gas exchange.

Big idea: the airways deliver air, but gas exchange only happens where air and blood are separated by a very thin wall: the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a function of the larynx?

choices.text: Enables the passage of air to the lungs
choices.explanation: Correct. Air flows through the larynx to reach the trachea and lungs.
Incorrect. The larynx does not filter carbon dioxide; carbon dioxide leaves the body by being breathed out.
Correct. The vocal cords are inside the larynx.

choices.text: Prevents food and liquids from traveling to the trachea
choices.explanation: Correct. The larynx and epiglottis close off the airway when you swallow.
Incorrect. The trachea is held open by its own C-shaped cartilage rings.

choices.text: Warms and moistens the transported air
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Warming and moistening the air is mainly the job of the nose and nasal cavity.

questions.explanation:
The answers are: it lets air pass to the lungs, it houses the vocal cords, and it keeps food and liquids out of the trachea. The larynx, or voice box, sits at the top of the trachea.

Air passes through the larynx on its way to the lungs. The vocal cords inside it vibrate to make sound. When you swallow, the larynx moves up and the epiglottis covers its opening so food goes down the esophagus instead of the windpipe. The larynx does not filter carbon dioxide (that is not something filtering does), and warming and moistening air is mainly done by the nose. The trachea is held open by its own cartilage rings, not by the larynx.

Big idea: the larynx has three main jobs: an airway, a voice box, and a guard that protects the lower airway when you swallow.

questions.prompt: The maximum amount of air moved in and out during a single breath is:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Alveolar ventilation is fresh air reaching the alveoli per minute, not one maximal breath.
Incorrect. This is not a lung volume.
Incorrect. Residual volume is air that always stays in the lungs and cannot be breathed out.
Incorrect. Tidal volume is a normal, quiet breath, not the maximum.
Incorrect. This is not a lung volume.
Correct. Vital capacity is the most air you can breathe out after the deepest breath in.

questions.explanation:
The answer is vital capacity. Vital capacity is the biggest amount of air you can move in one breath: breathe in as deeply as you can, then blow out as much as you can. It equals the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve volume plus the expiratory reserve volume.

Tidal volume is only a normal, relaxed breath (about 500 ml). Residual volume is the air that always stays in your lungs and can never be breathed out. Alveolar ventilation is how much fresh air reaches the alveoli each minute. 'Arterial flow restriction' and 'vascular limit' are not lung volumes.

Big idea: lung volumes and capacities describe how much air the lungs move and hold. Doctors measure them with a spirometer.

questions.prompt: What is the function of surfactant in the lungs?

choices.text: To expedite the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Surfactant does not speed up gas exchange itself; it keeps the sacs open.
Incorrect. Airflow depends on the airways' width, not on surfactant.

choices.text: To keep the alveoli from sticking together between breaths
choices.explanation: Correct. Surfactant lowers surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse and stick together.

choices.text: To push air into the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Air is drawn in by the diaphragm and chest muscles, not pushed by surfactant.

choices.text: To protect the villi from drying out
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Villi are in the small intestine, not the lungs.

choices.text: To seal the inner walls of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Surfactant does not seal the lungs; it keeps the alveoli open.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that surfactant keeps the alveoli from sticking together between breaths. The inside of each alveolus is coated with a thin layer of water. Water molecules pull on each other (surface tension), which tries to make the tiny sacs collapse and stick shut when you breathe out.

Surfactant, made by type II alveolar cells, is a soapy substance that lowers this surface tension. That keeps the alveoli open and makes them easier to inflate on the next breath. Surfactant does not speed up gas exchange directly or push air in, and villi are in the intestine, not the lungs.

Big idea: without surfactant, breathing takes enormous effort. That is why premature babies, who lack surfactant, can have serious breathing problems.

questions.prompt: How does the left lung compare to the right?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The left lung is smaller, so it is lighter, not heavier.
Correct. The left lung is smaller and lighter because the heart takes up room on the left.
Correct. The left lung is longer because the liver pushes the right side of the diaphragm up.
Correct. The left lung is narrower because the heart bulges into its space.
Incorrect. The right lung is the shorter one, because of the liver beneath it.
Incorrect. The left lung is narrower, not wider.

questions.explanation:
The answers are that the left lung is lighter, longer, and narrower. The heart sits slightly to the left in the chest, so the left lung has less room. It has only two lobes (the right has three) and a dent called the cardiac notch where the heart fits.

Because it is smaller, the left lung is lighter and narrower. It is also a bit longer, because the liver sits under the right side of the diaphragm and pushes the right side up, making the right lung shorter.

Big idea: organs fit together in the body. The heart and liver shape the lungs around them.

questions.prompt: When the inspiratory muscles contract:

choices.text: The thoracic cavity decreases in diameter
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Contracting inspiratory muscles make the chest wider, not narrower.

choices.text: The thoracic cavity decreases in length
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The diaphragm moves down, making the chest longer, not shorter.

choices.text: The thoracic cavity increases in diameter
choices.explanation: Correct. The external intercostals lift the ribs out, making the chest wider.

choices.text: The thoracic cavity increases in length
choices.explanation: Correct. The diaphragm flattens and moves down, making the chest longer.

choices.text: The volume of the thoracic cavity decreases
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The chest volume gets bigger during breathing in, not smaller.

choices.text: The volume of the thoracic cavity increases
choices.explanation: Correct. Wider and longer means the chest's volume increases, which pulls air in.

questions.explanation:
The answers are that the thoracic cavity gets wider, longer, and bigger in volume. The main inspiratory (breathing-in) muscles are the diaphragm and the external intercostal muscles between the ribs.

When the diaphragm contracts, it flattens and moves down, making the chest cavity longer. When the external intercostals contract, they lift the ribs up and out, making the chest wider. A bigger chest means a bigger volume, which lowers the pressure inside the lungs, so air flows in (Boyle's Law).

Big idea: breathing in is all about making the chest bigger to lower the pressure inside, so air rushes in from outside.

questions.prompt: Which of the following refers to the exchange of carbon dioxide and oxygen between systemic tissues and systemic capillaries?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. 'Acellular respiration' is not a real term.
Incorrect. Cellular respiration is the chemical process inside cells that uses oxygen to make energy, not the gas exchange itself.
Incorrect. External respiration is gas exchange in the lungs.
Correct. Internal respiration is gas exchange between the body's capillaries and tissues.
Incorrect. Pulmonary ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs.
Incorrect. 'Tidal ventilation' is not the term for gas exchange at the tissues.

questions.explanation:
The answer is internal respiration. There are several steps in respiration. Pulmonary ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs. External respiration is gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood in the lungs. Internal respiration is gas exchange between the blood in the body's capillaries and the body's tissues.

In internal respiration, oxygen leaves the blood and enters the tissue cells, and carbon dioxide leaves the cells and enters the blood. Cellular respiration is something different: it is the chemical process inside cells that uses oxygen to make energy.

Big idea: 'external' means at the lungs, and 'internal' means at the body's tissues.

questions.prompt: How is the majority of carbon dioxide carried in blood?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Gas bubbles in the blood are dangerous; CO2 does not travel this way.
Incorrect. Only about a fifth of CO2 is attached to red blood cells (as carbamino-hemoglobin).
Incorrect. About 20-23% of CO2 binds to hemoglobin, not the majority.
Incorrect. Very little CO2 is carried by plasma proteins.
Incorrect. Only about 7-10% of CO2 is dissolved in plasma.
Correct. About 70% of CO2 is carried as bicarbonate ions.

questions.explanation:
The answer is as bicarbonate ions. About 70% of carbon dioxide (CO2) travels in the blood as bicarbonate (HCO3-). Inside red blood cells, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase quickly combines CO2 with water to make carbonic acid, which splits into a hydrogen ion and bicarbonate.

The bicarbonate moves into the plasma and is carried to the lungs, where the reaction runs backward to release CO2 to be breathed out. About 20-23% of CO2 is bound to hemoglobin, and only about 7-10% is simply dissolved in the plasma. CO2 does not travel as bubbles.

Big idea: blood carries CO2 in three ways: as bicarbonate (most), bound to hemoglobin, and dissolved in plasma.

questions.prompt: Which two conditions most commonly contribute to COPD?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Asthma is a separate disease with airway narrowing that usually reverses.
Correct. Chronic bronchitis is one of the two main conditions that make up COPD.
Correct. Emphysema is the other main condition that makes up COPD.
Incorrect. Hyperventilation is fast breathing, not a cause of COPD.
Incorrect. Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs, not a part of COPD.
Incorrect. Sleep apnea is a breathing problem during sleep, not part of COPD.

questions.explanation:
The answers are chronic bronchitis and emphysema. COPD stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is a long-term lung disease that makes it hard to breathe out, usually caused by smoking.

Chronic bronchitis is long-term swelling of the airways with lots of mucus and coughing. Emphysema is damage to the walls of the alveoli, which makes the lungs floppy and traps air. Most people with COPD have a mix of both. Asthma also narrows the airways, but it usually comes and goes and is reversible, so it is considered a separate disease.

Big idea: COPD is an obstructive lung disease: air has trouble getting out of the lungs.

questions.prompt: High altitude can result in which of the following?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. COPD is caused mainly by smoking, not by altitude.
Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease.
Incorrect. Hyperoxia means too much oxygen; altitude causes too little.
Correct. Less oxygen in the air at altitude leads to hypoxia.
Incorrect. Pneumonia is a lung infection, not caused by altitude itself.

Incorrect for this question. Sleep apnea is usually caused by a blocked airway. Pauses in breathing during sleep can happen at very high altitude, but they are not the main effect this question is looking for.

questions.explanation:
The answer is hypoxia, which means the body's tissues are not getting enough oxygen. At high altitude the air pressure is lower, so each breath brings in less oxygen. Less oxygen enters the blood, and the tissues get less too.

The body responds by breathing faster and deeper and, over time, making more red blood cells. COPD, cystic fibrosis, and pneumonia are diseases with other causes. Hyperoxia (too much oxygen) is the opposite of what happens. Some people at very high altitude do get pauses in breathing while asleep, but the main expected effect is hypoxia.

Big idea: the higher you go, the lower the oxygen pressure in the air, so getting enough oxygen becomes harder.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a function of the respiratory system?

choices.explanation: Correct. Changing how much CO2 is breathed out helps control blood pH.
Incorrect. Body temperature is mainly controlled by the skin and blood vessels, not the lungs.
Correct. Gas exchange is the main job of the respiratory system.
Correct. The larynx produces sound for speech.

questions.explanation:
The answers are blood pH regulation, gas exchange, and speech. The respiratory system's main job is gas exchange: bringing in oxygen and removing carbon dioxide.

By breathing out more or less carbon dioxide, the lungs also help control the blood's pH (CO2 makes blood more acidic). The larynx and vocal cords produce sound for speech. Some heat is lost in breath, but temperature regulation is mainly the job of the skin and blood vessels, so it is not counted as a main respiratory function here.

Big idea: the respiratory system does more than breathing: it also controls blood pH and allows speech and smell.

questions.prompt: When the muscles are voluntarily contracted to breathe, it is called

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Quiet breathing is normal, relaxed breathing.
Incorrect. 'Voluntary breathing' is not the standard term.
Incorrect. 'Controlled breathing' is not the standard term.
Correct. Forced breathing uses extra muscles to breathe more deeply or forcefully.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is forced breathing. Quiet breathing is normal, relaxed breathing: the diaphragm and external intercostals contract to breathe in, and breathing out is passive.

Forced (deep or labored) breathing happens during exercise, or when you choose to take a big breath or blow out hard. Extra muscles join in: neck and chest muscles help you breathe in, and abdominal and internal intercostal muscles push air out. 'Voluntary breathing' and 'controlled breathing' are not the standard names for this.

Big idea: quiet breathing uses just the main muscles; forced breathing adds accessory muscles.

questions.prompt: Which of the following muscles help in inspiration?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The pectoralis minor can help only during forced breathing; it is not a main inspiration muscle.
Correct. The diaphragm is the main muscle of breathing in.
Correct. The external intercostals lift the ribs to help breathe in.
Incorrect. The internal intercostals help push air out during forced breathing.

questions.explanation:
The answers are the diaphragm and the external intercostals. These are the main muscles of inspiration (breathing in).

The diaphragm contracts and flattens, making the chest longer. The external intercostals lift the ribs up and out, making the chest wider. The pectoralis minor can help a little during forced breathing, but it is not a main breathing muscle. The internal intercostals pull the ribs down and help with forced breathing out.

Big idea: breathing in means making the chest bigger; the diaphragm and external intercostals do this.

questions.prompt: What is residual volume?

choices.text: The normal amount of air that is exhaled or inhaled
choices.explanation: Incorrect. That describes tidal volume.

choices.text: The maximum amount of air that can be inspired after breathing in normally
choices.explanation: Incorrect. That describes inspiratory reserve volume.

choices.text: The maximum amount of air that can be exhaled after breathing out normally
choices.explanation: Incorrect. That describes expiratory reserve volume.

choices.text: The volume of air remaining in the lungs after forced expiration
choices.explanation: Correct. Residual volume is the air left after breathing out as much as possible.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after forced expiration. Even after you blow out as hard as you can, about 1-1.2 liters of air stays in your lungs. This is the residual volume.

Residual volume keeps the alveoli from collapsing and lets gas exchange continue between breaths. The other choices describe tidal volume (a normal breath), inspiratory reserve volume (extra air in), and expiratory reserve volume (extra air out).

Big idea: you can never empty your lungs completely; the leftover air is the residual volume.

questions.prompt: With an increase in BPG at high altitude, hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen _________

choices.explanation: Incorrect. More BPG makes hemoglobin hold oxygen less tightly.
Correct. BPG decreases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
Incorrect. BPG does change hemoglobin's affinity.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that hemoglobin's affinity (grip) for oxygen decreases. BPG (2,3-bisphosphoglycerate) is a chemical inside red blood cells that sticks to hemoglobin and makes it let go of oxygen more easily.

At high altitude, the body makes more BPG. This shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right, so hemoglobin releases more oxygen to the tissues, which helps them get enough oxygen even though there is less oxygen in the air.

Big idea: the body adjusts how tightly hemoglobin holds oxygen. Loosening the grip helps deliver oxygen to tissues.

questions.prompt: _______ nerves are responsible for the contraction and relaxation of the diaphragm

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The vagus nerve goes to the heart, lungs, and gut, but it does not move the diaphragm.
Correct. The phrenic nerves control the diaphragm.
Incorrect. The intercostal nerves control the muscles between the ribs.
Incorrect. The splanchnic nerves go to the abdominal organs.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the (motor) phrenic nerves. The phrenic nerves come from the neck (spinal nerves C3, C4, and C5) and run down to the diaphragm.

They carry the signals that make the diaphragm contract. A memory phrase: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.' The vagus nerve carries signals to many organs but does not control the diaphragm, the intercostal nerves control the rib muscles, and the splanchnic nerves go to the abdominal organs.

Big idea: breathing depends on nerves from the brain and spinal cord. Damage to the phrenic nerves can paralyze the diaphragm.

questions.prompt: Alveoli are lined with

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Simple columnar cells are tall; they line the stomach and intestines.
Correct. Thin, flat simple squamous cells allow fast gas exchange.
Incorrect. Simple cuboidal cells are cube-shaped and found in glands and kidney tubules.
Incorrect. Stratified epithelium has many layers, which would be too thick.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is simple squamous epithelium. 'Simple' means one layer of cells, and 'squamous' means flat cells.

The alveoli need a very thin wall so gases can diffuse quickly between the air and the blood. A single layer of flat cells (type I alveolar cells) is as thin as possible. Columnar and cuboidal cells are taller and thicker, and stratified means many layers, which would slow gas exchange.

Big idea: structure matches function. Thin, flat cells are perfect for diffusion.

questions.prompt: The lungs are divided into lobes: the right with ____ and the left with _____

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This reverses the numbers.
Incorrect. The right lung has three lobes, not two.
Correct. Right lung: 3 lobes; left lung: 2 lobes.
Incorrect. The left lung has only two lobes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 3 lobes on the right and 2 on the left. A lobe is a large section of a lung separated by deep grooves called fissures.

The right lung has a superior, middle, and inferior lobe. The left lung has only a superior and inferior lobe, because the heart leans to the left and takes up some of the space. The left lung has a dent called the cardiac notch where the heart fits.

Big idea: the two lungs are not identical; the left is smaller because of the heart.

questions.prompt: How many O2 molecules can bind to a hemoglobin molecule?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Hemoglobin has four binding sites, not one.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin has four binding sites, not two.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin has four binding sites, not three.
Correct. Each of hemoglobin's four heme groups binds one O2 molecule.
Incorrect. There are only four heme groups.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 4. Hemoglobin is made of four protein chains, and each chain holds one heme group with an iron atom in the middle.

Each iron atom can bind one oxygen molecule (O2), so one hemoglobin molecule can carry 4 oxygen molecules. When one oxygen binds, it becomes easier for the next ones to bind, which is called cooperative binding.

Big idea: hemoglobin is the oxygen carrier in red blood cells, and its four binding sites let it carry lots of oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which of the following structures is included in the conducting zone?

choices.explanation: Correct. The larynx is an air passage in the conducting zone.
Correct. Bronchioles (down to the terminal bronchioles) carry air and belong to the conducting zone.
Correct. The bronchi carry air into the lungs.
Correct. The trachea carries air to the bronchi.
Correct. All four structures are in the conducting zone.

questions.note: The official key leaves out bronchioles, but bronchioles (down to the terminal bronchioles) belong to the conducting zone, so all four structures, and "All of the above", are correct.
questions.explanation:
All the choices are correct: the larynx, bronchioles, bronchi, trachea, and 'All of the above'. The conducting zone is the set of airways that carry air to the gas exchange areas, warming, moistening, and cleaning it along the way.

It runs from the nose and pharynx through the larynx, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles, ending at the terminal bronchioles. Only when alveoli appear (respiratory bronchioles and beyond) does the respiratory zone begin. The official key left out bronchioles, but ordinary and terminal bronchioles are conducting airways.

Big idea: conducting zone = air tubes; respiratory zone = gas exchange areas with alveoli.

questions.prompt: Which gas law states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the pressures exerted by each gas in the mixture?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Henry's Law is about how much gas dissolves in a liquid.
Correct. Dalton's Law: total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures.
Incorrect. Boyle's Law links pressure and volume.
Incorrect. Charles' Law links volume and temperature.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is Dalton's Law. Dalton's Law says the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the pressures of each gas in it. Each gas's share is its partial pressure.

Air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, so at sea level (760 mmHg) oxygen's partial pressure is about 0.21 x 760, roughly 160 mmHg. Henry's Law is about gases dissolving in liquids, Boyle's Law about pressure and volume, and Charles' Law about volume and temperature.

Big idea: partial pressures drive gas exchange. Gases move from where their partial pressure is high to where it is low.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is true about cystic fibrosis?

choices.explanation: Correct. CF is autosomal recessive: two faulty copies are needed.

choices.text: Commonly prevalent in northern or central Europeans
choices.explanation: Correct. CF is most common in people of northern and central European ancestry.
Correct. Thick mucus blocks the pancreas and damages it.

choices.text: Average lifespan of those affected is around 50 years old
choices.explanation: Not counted by this key. Life expectancy with CF keeps rising with new treatments, so a fixed 'around 50' is not reliable.
Incorrect. The key does not count choice D as correct.

questions.explanation:
The answers are: the CF gene is recessive, it is most common in people of northern or central European ancestry, and it affects cells in the pancreas. Cystic fibrosis is an inherited disease. A person needs two faulty copies of the CFTR gene (one from each parent) to have it, which is what 'recessive' means.

CF is most common in people with northern European ancestry. Thick mucus blocks the pancreas, so digestive enzymes cannot reach the intestine. Life expectancy has been improving quickly with new treatments; people born recently are expected to live into their 50s or longer, so 'around 50' is not a fixed fact and was not counted as correct by this key.

Big idea: CF affects both the respiratory and digestive systems because both rely on mucus and fluid secretions.

questions.prompt: Emphysema is characterized by

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Excess mucus is the main sign of chronic bronchitis.
Incorrect. Emphysema affects the alveoli, not the larynx and trachea.
Incorrect. Mycobacterium causes tuberculosis, which is an infection.
Correct. In emphysema, alveolar walls break down, leaving permanently enlarged air spaces.
Incorrect. One of the listed choices is right, so 'None of the above' does not apply.

questions.explanation:
The answer is permanent enlargement of the alveoli. In emphysema, usually caused by smoking, the thin walls between alveoli are destroyed. Many small air sacs merge into fewer, bigger, floppy ones.

This reduces the surface area for gas exchange, and the lungs lose their springiness, so air gets trapped and breathing out is hard. Excess mucus describes chronic bronchitis. Swelling of the larynx and trachea is not emphysema, and Mycobacterium causes tuberculosis.

Big idea: emphysema destroys alveoli, reducing gas exchange area. It is one of the two main parts of COPD.

questions.prompt: What molecule carries O2 and CO2? How does this molecule's affinity for oxygen change when oxygen binds to it initially? What about CO2?
questions.answer: Hemoglobin carries these molecules. When oxygen binds to it, its affinity for oxygen increases, making it easier for more oxygen to bind. When CO2 binds, its affinity for oxygen decreases.
questions.explanation:
Hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells, carries both oxygen and some carbon dioxide. Each hemoglobin can hold four oxygen molecules.

When the first oxygen binds, hemoglobin changes shape so the next oxygens bind more easily. This is called cooperative binding, and it makes hemoglobin quickly fill up in the lungs. When CO2 (and acid) bind, hemoglobin's grip on oxygen loosens, so it releases oxygen more easily in the tissues. This is the Bohr effect.

Big idea: hemoglobin grabs oxygen in the lungs and lets it go where CO2 is high, which is exactly where cells need oxygen.

questions.prompt: What cells secrete surfactants? What function does surfactants play in gas exchange?
questions.answer: Type II alveolar cells secrete surfactants, which reduces surface tension of alveolar fluid prevent alveolar collapse when exhaling.
questions.explanation:
Surfactant is made by type II alveolar cells (type II pneumocytes). It is a slippery mix of fats (phospholipids) and proteins.

The inside of each alveolus is coated with a thin layer of water, and the pull between water molecules (surface tension) tries to collapse the tiny sacs. Surfactant lowers this surface tension, so the alveoli stay open when you breathe out and are easy to inflate again. Open alveoli keep a large surface area available for gas exchange.

Big idea: surfactant keeps the alveoli open so gas exchange can continue.

questions.prompt: What roles do sinuses play in respiration? Name the four different sinuses
questions.answer: They help to warm and moisten incoming air as to not damage the more sensitive lung tissue. There is the ethmoid, maxillary, frontal, and sphenoid sinus.
questions.explanation:
The paranasal sinuses are air-filled spaces in the skull bones around the nose. They make mucus that drains into the nasal cavity, which helps warm, moisten, and filter the air you breathe in so it does not irritate the delicate lungs.

They also make the skull lighter and help give the voice its sound (resonance). The four pairs are the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid sinuses, each named for the bone it sits in.

Big idea: the upper respiratory tract prepares air (warm, moist, clean) before it reaches the lungs.

questions.prompt: What role does the cilia lining play within the respiratory system?
questions.answer: They help to move microbes and debris that are caught in the mucus up and out of the bronchi.
questions.explanation:
Cilia are tiny hair-like structures on the cells lining most of the airways. Goblet cells make sticky mucus that traps dust, germs, and other particles.

The cilia beat together in waves, moving the mucus upward toward the throat, like an escalator (the 'mucociliary escalator'). There it is swallowed or coughed out. This keeps the lungs clean. Smoking damages cilia, which is one reason smokers cough a lot.

Big idea: mucus and cilia work as a team to protect the lungs from dirt and germs.

questions.prompt: What are the three divisions of the pharynx? Include the structures associated with each region
questions.answer: Nasopharynx- upper division between skull base and soft palate (nasal cavity), oropharynx- region behind base of tongue between soft palate and esophagus, laryngopharynx- behind epiglottis/cricoid cartilage
questions.explanation:
The pharynx (throat) has three parts. The nasopharynx is the top part, behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. It carries only air and contains the adenoids (pharyngeal tonsil).

The oropharynx is the middle part, behind the mouth, from the soft palate down to the epiglottis. It carries both air and food and contains the palatine tonsils. The laryngopharynx is the bottom part, behind the larynx, which leads into both the esophagus and the larynx.

Big idea: the pharynx is shared by the respiratory and digestive systems, and each part has its own neighbors and tonsils.

questions.prompt: Air rushes into the lungs during inhalation because

choices.text: the rib muscles and diaphragm contract, increasing the lung volume.
choices.explanation: Correct. Contracting muscles enlarge the chest and lungs, lowering pressure so air flows in.
Incorrect. During inhalation, pressure in the alveoli decreases, which pulls air in.

choices.text: gas flows from a region of lower pressure to a region of higher pressure
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Gas flows from higher pressure to lower pressure, not the other way.

choices.text: pulmonary muscles contract and pull on the outer surface of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The lungs have no 'pulmonary muscles'; they are pulled open by the chest wall.

choices.text: a positive respiratory pressure is created when the diaphragm relaxes
choices.explanation: Incorrect. When the diaphragm relaxes, you breathe out, not in.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the rib muscles and diaphragm contract, increasing the lung volume. When the diaphragm contracts it moves down, and when the external intercostal muscles contract they lift the ribs. Both make the chest, and the lungs inside it, bigger.

When the lungs get bigger, the air inside spreads out and its pressure drops below the air pressure outside the body (Boyle's Law). Gas always flows from higher pressure to lower pressure, so air rushes in. The lungs have no muscles of their own; they are pulled open by the chest.

Big idea: breathing works by changing the chest's volume to change the pressure inside the lungs.

questions.prompt: Breathing is usually regulated by

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Widening of the bronchi affects airflow, not the control of breathing.

choices.text: the concentration of red blood cells
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Red blood cell count does not directly control breathing.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin level does not directly control breathing rate.

choices.text: CO2 and O2 concentration and pH-level sensors
choices.explanation: Correct. Chemoreceptors sense CO2, O2, and pH and adjust breathing.
Incorrect. The larynx and lungs move air, but the brainstem controls breathing.

questions.explanation:
The answer is CO2 and O2 concentration and pH-level sensors. Special sensors called chemoreceptors watch the blood's chemistry and tell the brainstem how fast and deep to breathe.

Central chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond mostly to carbon dioxide and pH. Peripheral chemoreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries also sense low oxygen. When CO2 rises (and pH falls), you breathe faster and deeper to blow off the extra CO2. Red blood cell count, hemoglobin levels, and the airways themselves do not set your breathing rate.

Big idea: breathing is controlled automatically by the brainstem, mainly in response to carbon dioxide levels in the blood.

questions.prompt: Which one of these statements about lungs is false?

choices.text: Gas exchange takes place across moist membranes.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this statement is true). Gases must dissolve in a moist layer to cross the membrane.

choices.text: The gases move across the exchange membranes by diffusion.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this statement is true). Gases cross the membrane by diffusion.

choices.text: The total exchange surface area is relatively large.
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this statement is true). The lungs have a huge exchange surface, about the size of a tennis court.

choices.text: The lining of the alveoli is only one cell thick
choices.explanation: Incorrect (this statement is true). Alveolar walls are a single layer of thin cells.

choices.text: The concentration of CO2 is higher in the air than in the alveolar capillaries.
choices.explanation: Correct (this is the false statement). CO2 is higher in the capillary blood than in the alveolar air.

questions.explanation:
The false statement is that the concentration of CO2 is higher in the air than in the alveolar capillaries. It is the other way around: the blood arriving at the lungs has more CO2 than the air in the alveoli.

That is why CO2 diffuses out of the blood and into the alveoli, where it is breathed out. All the other statements are true: gas exchange happens across moist membranes, by diffusion, over a very large surface area, through walls only one cell thick.

Big idea: gases diffuse from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. Oxygen moves into the blood; carbon dioxide moves out.

questions.prompt: The structure labeled "X" on the diagram below is the ____________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The epiglottis is a small flap above the larynx.
Incorrect. The pharynx is the throat, higher up behind the nose and mouth.
Correct. X points to the ringed tube in the neck, the trachea.
Incorrect. The larynx is the voice box just above the trachea.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the trachea. In the diagram, X points to the tube running down the middle of the neck into the chest, with ring-like stripes. Those stripes are the C-shaped cartilage rings of the trachea (windpipe).

The trachea carries air from the larynx down to the bronchi. The larynx is the boxy part above it, the pharynx is the throat behind the nose and mouth, and the epiglottis is the small flap above the larynx.

Big idea: the rings of cartilage keep the trachea open so air can always flow.

questions.prompt: Alveoli in the lungs are connected to the bronchi by a network of tiny tubes called ___________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Arterioles are small arteries that carry blood.
Correct. Bronchioles connect the bronchi to the alveoli.
Incorrect. Capillaries are tiny blood vessels around the alveoli.
Incorrect. Venules are small veins that carry blood.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bronchioles. The bronchi branch into smaller and smaller tubes called bronchioles, which carry air to the alveoli.

Arterioles, capillaries, and venules are blood vessels, not airways. They carry blood, not air.

Big idea: the airways branch like a tree: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and finally alveoli.

questions.prompt: The actual exchange of gases occurs at the site of the

choices.explanation: Correct. Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli.
Incorrect. The nasal passages warm and clean air but do not exchange gases.
Incorrect. The larynx is an air passage and voice box.
Incorrect. The trachea carries air but its walls are too thick for gas exchange.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the alveoli. The alveoli are tiny air sacs with walls only one cell thick, surrounded by capillaries.

Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. The nasal passages, larynx, and trachea only carry air.

Big idea: gas exchange needs a thin, moist, large surface, which is exactly what the alveoli provide.

questions.prompt: Gas exchange occurs when

choices.text: oxygen in the alveoli diffuses into the blood in the capillaries.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. This is true, but the other steps are also part of gas exchange.

choices.text: oxygen binds with hemoglobin in the red blood cells .
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. This is true, but so are the other statements.

choices.text: the red blood cells give up oxygen in the cells on the body tissues.
choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. This is true, but so are the other statements.
Correct. All three describe parts of gas exchange.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'all of the above'. Gas exchange includes several connected steps: oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, oxygen binds to hemoglobin in red blood cells, and red blood cells release oxygen to the body's tissues.

The first step happens in the lungs (external respiration), and the last happens in the tissues (internal respiration). Hemoglobin carries the oxygen between them.

Big idea: oxygen's journey goes from the air, into the blood, onto hemoglobin, and finally into the cells that need it.

questions.prompt: When the diaphragm and rib cage muscles relax,

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Relaxing these muscles makes the chest smaller.
Incorrect. Inspiration happens when these muscles contract.
Correct. Relaxing muscles shrink the chest and push air out.
Incorrect. Breathing continues; relaxing is how you breathe out.
Incorrect. Relaxing breathing muscles does not constrict the bronchi.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that expiration occurs. When the diaphragm and rib muscles relax, the diaphragm moves back up and the ribs drop down. The chest gets smaller.

A smaller chest squeezes the lungs, raising the pressure inside them above the outside air pressure, so air flows out. During quiet breathing, breathing out is passive: it just needs the muscles to relax. The bronchi do not constrict from this.

Big idea: muscles contract to breathe in and relax to breathe out (during quiet breathing).

questions.prompt: Which of the following occurs as air rushes into the lungs from the environment to equalize air pressure?

choices.explanation: Correct. Inspiration is air flowing into the lungs.
Incorrect. Contraction is what muscles do, not the name of air flowing in.
Incorrect. Expiration is breathing out.
Incorrect. Dilation means widening.
Incorrect. Constriction means narrowing.

questions.explanation:
The answer is inspiration. Inspiration means breathing in. When the chest gets bigger, pressure inside the lungs drops below the outside air pressure, and air rushes in until the pressures are equal.

Expiration is breathing out. Contraction, dilation, and constriction are words for muscle or tube actions, not the name for air flowing in.

Big idea: air moves into and out of the lungs to equalize pressure.

questions.prompt: The dome - shaped muscle below the chest cavity is called the _________________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The trachea is the windpipe.
Incorrect. The pharynx is the throat.
Correct. The diaphragm is the dome-shaped breathing muscle.
Incorrect. The larynx is the voice box.
Incorrect. The epiglottis is a flap that covers the larynx.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the diaphragm. The diaphragm is a dome-shaped sheet of skeletal muscle that separates the chest from the abdomen.

It is the main muscle of breathing. When it contracts, it flattens and moves down, making room for the lungs to expand. The trachea, pharynx, larynx, and epiglottis are airway structures, not muscles below the chest.

Big idea: the diaphragm does most of the work of quiet breathing.

questions.prompt: Which of the following provides a passage for both food and air?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The esophagus carries only food.
Incorrect. The trachea carries only air.
Correct. The pharynx carries both food and air.
Incorrect. The larynx carries only air.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pharynx (throat). Air from the nose and food from the mouth both pass through the pharynx.

Below the pharynx, the paths split: air goes into the larynx and trachea, and food goes into the esophagus. The epiglottis keeps food from going the wrong way.

Big idea: the pharynx is shared by the respiratory and digestive systems.

questions.prompt: All are functions of the larynx except

choices.text: Serves as a passageway for food.
choices.explanation: Correct. Food does not pass through the larynx.

choices.text: Protects the airway from choking on material in the throat .
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The larynx does protect the airway.

choices.text: Regulates the flow of air into the lungs.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Air does pass through the larynx into the lungs.
Incorrect. The larynx does produce sound.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'serves as a passageway for food'. The question asks what the larynx does NOT do. Food goes through the pharynx and then into the esophagus, not through the larynx.

The larynx protects the airway (the epiglottis covers it when you swallow, and coughing clears it), lets air flow into the lungs, and produces sound with the vocal cords.

Big idea: the larynx is an airway and voice box; food should never pass through it.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 1 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 1 is the pharynx (throat). It is the passage behind the nose and mouth that air and food both travel through.

Air goes from the pharynx into the larynx and trachea; food goes from the pharynx into the esophagus.

Big idea: the pharynx is shared by the respiratory and digestive systems.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 2 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 2 is the esophagus, the muscular tube that runs behind the trachea and carries food from the pharynx to the stomach.

In the diagram it is the tube just behind the windpipe in the neck. Food moves down it by peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction.

Big idea: the esophagus and trachea run side by side; the epiglottis makes sure food goes into the esophagus.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 3 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 3 is the pulmonary arteries, the blue vessels entering the lungs.

Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs, so they are drawn blue. This is the opposite of most arteries, which carry oxygen-rich blood.

Big idea: arteries carry blood away from the heart; in the lungs, that blood is low in oxygen.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 4 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 4 is the pulmonary veins, the red vessels leaving the lungs.

Pulmonary veins carry oxygen-rich blood from the lungs back to the heart, so they are drawn red.

Big idea: veins carry blood toward the heart; in the lungs, that blood has just picked up oxygen.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 5 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 5 points to the alveoli, the tiny air sacs that fill the lungs.

The alveoli are where oxygen moves into the blood and carbon dioxide moves out. Millions of them give the lungs a huge surface for gas exchange.

Big idea: the alveoli are the gas exchange surface of the lungs.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 6 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 6 is the trachea (windpipe), the tube in the neck below the larynx.

The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage and carries air down to the bronchi.

Big idea: cartilage rings keep the airway open so air can always flow.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 7 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 7 is smooth muscle, the bands wrapped around the bronchiole.

Smooth muscle in the bronchioles can tighten (narrowing the airway) or relax (widening it). In an asthma attack, this muscle tightens too much.

Big idea: bronchioles control airflow using smooth muscle, which inhalers relax.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 8 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 8 is an alveolar duct, the short passage leading from the respiratory bronchiole into the clusters of alveoli.

Its walls are made mostly of alveoli, so it is part of the respiratory zone where gas exchange happens.

Big idea: air flows from respiratory bronchioles into alveolar ducts, then into alveolar sacs.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure labeled 9 in the diagram.
questions.explanation:
Label 9 is the alveolar sacs, the grape-like clusters of alveoli at the end of the airway.

Each sac is a group of alveoli sharing a common opening. Wrapped in capillaries, they provide a huge area for gas exchange.

Big idea: clusters of alveoli maximize the surface area of the lungs.

questions.prompt: Where in the lungs does the exchange of O2 and CO2 for blood occur?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Smooth muscle changes the width of airways; it does not exchange gases.
Correct. Gas exchange happens across the walls of the alveoli.
Incorrect. Bronchi only carry air.
Incorrect. Elastic fibers help the lungs spring back; they do not exchange gases.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the alveoli. Alveoli are tiny air sacs with walls one cell thick, wrapped in capillaries.

Oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses out. Smooth muscle and elastic fibers help control and support the airways, and the bronchi only carry air.

Big idea: gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Which abnormal breathing pattern is represented in the figure above?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Biot breathing has clusters of equal-sized breaths, not waxing and waning.
Incorrect. Ataxic breathing is completely irregular.
Incorrect. Apneustic breathing has long, held breaths in.
Correct. Breaths grow, shrink, then stop: the Cheyne-Stokes pattern.

questions.explanation:
The answer is Cheyne-Stokes breathing. In the figure, the breaths get bigger and bigger, then smaller and smaller, followed by a pause with no breathing (apnea), and then the pattern repeats.

This crescendo-decrescendo pattern with pauses is Cheyne-Stokes breathing, often seen in heart failure or brain injury. Biot breathing has groups of equal deep breaths separated by pauses, ataxic breathing is completely irregular, and apneustic breathing has long gasping breaths in.

Big idea: abnormal breathing patterns have recognizable shapes that point to problems in breathing control.

questions.prompt: Which time points on the figure (V-Z) are associated with the lowest PCO2 of lung blood?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. At V breathing has just started, so CO2 is still high.
Incorrect. At W breathing is strong, but CO2 has not yet fallen to its lowest.
Incorrect. At X CO2 is falling but is not yet at its lowest.
Correct. Right after the long burst of breathing ends, lung-blood CO2 is at its lowest.
Incorrect. At Z CO2 has built up during the pause and is high again.

questions.explanation:
The answer is Y. During the burst of deep breathing (V to X), the lungs blow off lots of carbon dioxide, so the blood leaving the lungs has less and less CO2.

At point Y, breathing has just stopped after the long burst of over-breathing, so the lung blood still has very little CO2: it is at its lowest. During the pause, CO2 slowly builds back up, which eventually triggers the next round of breathing at Z. In Cheyne-Stokes breathing, the brain senses CO2 with a delay, which is why the cycle overshoots.

Big idea: breathing removes CO2, and the brain uses CO2 levels to decide how hard to breathe.

questions.prompt: Assuming a respiratory rate of 14 breaths/min, calculate the minute ventilation.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This is much too small for 14 breaths of 0.5 L.
Incorrect. This is too small; 0.5 x 14 = 7.
Incorrect. This is close but does not match 0.5 x 14.
Correct. 0.5 L x 14 breaths/min = 7 L/min.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 7 L/min. Minute ventilation is how much air you breathe in one minute: tidal volume x breathing rate.

In the graph, normal breaths go up and down between about 3.0 and 3.5 liters, so the tidal volume is about 0.5 L. 0.5 L x 14 breaths/min = 7 L/min.

Big idea: minute ventilation = tidal volume x respiratory rate.

questions.prompt: A residual volume of 1.5 liter was determined using the helium dilution technique. What is the FRC (in liters)?

choices.explanation: Correct. ERV (2 L) + RV (1.5 L) = 3.5 L.
Incorrect. 2.0 L is only the expiratory reserve volume.
Incorrect. 1.0 L is where the lowest breath out reaches on the graph, not the FRC.
Incorrect. This is much too small.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 3.5 liters. Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the amount of air left in the lungs after a normal breath out. It equals the expiratory reserve volume (ERV) plus the residual volume (RV).

In the graph, normal breaths out end at about 3 liters, and a maximal breath out goes down to 1 liter, so the ERV is 3 - 1 = 2 liters. FRC = ERV + RV = 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 liters. (The graph's 'zero' is not the true bottom of the lungs, because spirometry cannot measure residual volume; that is why the helium test is needed.)

Big idea: spirometers cannot measure residual volume, so other tests like helium dilution are used to find FRC.

questions.prompt: Which dissociation curve shows a (red line) for normal blood and a (green line) for blood that has carbon monoxide?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Here the green line is lower but shifted right, which does not match CO.
Incorrect. This shows a right shift, as in exercise.
Incorrect. This shows a left shift, as in fetal blood.
Incorrect. This shows only a small change, not CO's large drop.
Correct. The green line is shifted left and levels off much lower, as with CO.
Incorrect. The two lines are almost the same.

questions.explanation:
The answer is E. Carbon monoxide (CO) binds to hemoglobin about 200-250 times more tightly than oxygen. That leaves fewer spots for oxygen, so the curve's maximum saturation drops (the green line flattens out lower).

CO also makes the remaining oxygen stick more tightly, shifting the curve to the left. Graph E shows both: a green line that rises early (left) but levels off much lower.

Big idea: carbon monoxide is dangerous because it blocks oxygen from binding and stops hemoglobin from releasing the oxygen it does carry.

questions.prompt: Which dissociation curve shows a (red line) for blood when a person is at rest and a (green line) for blood when a person is exercising?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The green line is lower overall, which matches CO, not exercise.
Correct. The exercise curve is shifted to the right.
Incorrect. This shows a left shift.
Incorrect. This shows a left shift, not a right shift.
Incorrect. This shows a much lower maximum, as with CO.
Incorrect. The curves are almost the same.

questions.explanation:
The answer is B. During exercise, muscles are warmer, more acidic, and make more carbon dioxide. All of these shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right.

A right shift means hemoglobin lets go of oxygen more easily, which delivers more oxygen to working muscles. In graph B, the green (exercise) curve is to the right of the red (rest) curve, with the same top.

Big idea: right shift = release more oxygen (exercise, heat, acid, CO2); left shift = hold oxygen tighter.

questions.prompt: Which dissociation curve shows a (red line) which is blood from an adult and a (green line) which is blood from a fetus?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This shows a much lower maximum, not a fetal curve.
Incorrect. This shows a right shift.
Correct. The fetal curve is shifted to the left.
Incorrect. The difference here is too small and not a clear left shift.
Incorrect. This shows a much lower maximum, as with CO.
Incorrect. The curves are almost the same.

questions.explanation:
The answer is C. Fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly than adult hemoglobin, so the fetal curve is shifted to the left.

This lets the fetus pull oxygen from the mother's blood across the placenta. In graph C, the green (fetal) curve rises earlier, to the left of the red (adult) curve, and both reach the same top.

Big idea: a left shift means higher affinity for oxygen, which helps the fetus grab oxygen from the mother.

questions.prompt: Which point represents arterial blood in a critically anemic person?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Point A is no oxygen at all.
Incorrect. Point B is low PO2, like in very active tissue.
Incorrect. Point C is around the PO2 of venous blood.
Correct. Arterial blood is nearly fully saturated, even in anemia.
Incorrect. Point E is on the lower curve, which does not describe normal arterial saturation in anemia.

questions.explanation:
The answer is D. In anemia, a person has too little hemoglobin, but the hemoglobin they do have still fills up with oxygen normally in the lungs.

The graph's y-axis is oxygen saturation (the percent of hemoglobin carrying oxygen). Arterial blood at a normal PO2 of about 100 mmHg is nearly 100% saturated even in anemia, which is point D. The total amount of oxygen in the blood is low, but the saturation is normal.

Big idea: saturation is a percent; anemia lowers how much hemoglobin there is, not how full each hemoglobin is.

questions.prompt: Stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system would increase airway resistance.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The sympathetic nervous system is the 'fight or flight' system. During stress or exercise, it relaxes the smooth muscle in the bronchioles, widening them (bronchodilation).

Wider airways mean LESS airway resistance, so more air can flow. That is also why asthma inhalers use drugs (beta-2 agonists) that copy this sympathetic effect.

Big idea: the sympathetic system opens the airways; the parasympathetic system narrows them.

questions.prompt: The medulla oblongata contains neurons which control breathing.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. The medulla oblongata, in the brainstem, contains the main breathing centers: the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups.

These neurons set the basic rhythm of breathing and send signals to the diaphragm and rib muscles. The pons above helps fine-tune the rhythm.

Big idea: breathing is controlled automatically by the brainstem.

questions.prompt: During heavy breathing, extra force can be achieved by contraction of these muscles (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is the abdominal muscles. During quiet breathing, breathing out is passive. During heavy breathing (like exercise), the abdominal muscles contract.

This pushes the abdominal organs up against the diaphragm and pulls the ribs down, squeezing air out of the lungs faster and more forcefully. The internal intercostal muscles help too.

Big idea: forced expiration uses abdominal muscles to push air out.

questions.prompt: This thin layer of fluid lubricates the movement of the lungs within the thoracic cavity (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is pleural (pleural fluid). Each lung is wrapped in a two-layer membrane called the pleura.

A thin film of pleural fluid between the layers acts like a lubricant, letting the lungs slide smoothly against the chest wall as they expand and shrink. It also helps the lungs stick to the chest wall so they expand when the chest expands.

Big idea: the pleura and pleural fluid protect the lungs and help them move during breathing.

questions.prompt: This method of movement allows exchange of O2 into pulmonary blood and CO2 in the opposite direction (one word)
questions.explanation:
The answer is diffusion. Diffusion is the movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration (or partial pressure) to lower.

Oxygen is higher in the alveoli than in the blood arriving at the lungs, so it diffuses into the blood. Carbon dioxide is higher in the blood, so it diffuses into the alveoli. No energy is needed.

Big idea: gas exchange in the lungs happens by simple diffusion.

questions.prompt: What is inside the inhaler to treat asthma?
questions.context: A patient who has previously had COVID a week prior to coming into the ER claims she cannot exercise without feeling like she cannot breathe. You note that she has asthma cause by COVID and will prescribe an inhaler for her.
questions.explanation:
The answer is beta-2 agonists. A rescue inhaler for asthma usually contains a beta-2 agonist, such as albuterol.

Beta-2 agonists act like the body's 'fight or flight' signals on the airways. Many inhalers for long-term control contain corticosteroids instead, which reduce inflammation.

Big idea: asthma inhalers either open the airways (beta-2 agonists) or calm inflammation (steroids).

questions.prompt: How does the inhaler treat asthma?
questions.context: A patient who has previously had COVID a week prior to coming into the ER claims she cannot exercise without feeling like she cannot breathe. You note that she has asthma cause by COVID and will prescribe an inhaler for her.
questions.answer: The Beta-2 agonists will relax the smooth muscles of the bronchi to provide relief
questions.explanation:
Beta-2 agonists bind to beta-2 receptors on the smooth muscle around the bronchioles. This makes the muscle relax.

In an asthma attack, this smooth muscle tightens and narrows the airways. Relaxing it widens the airways (bronchodilation), so air flows more easily and breathing gets easier within minutes.

Big idea: asthma is airway narrowing, and relaxing airway smooth muscle reverses it.

questions.prompt: A patient claims progressive shortness of breath over 6 months. You run pulmonary function tests which show an increase in residual volume, decrease in diffusion capacity, and decrease forced expiratory volume / forced vital capacity ratio. You take an x-ray and find the lower lobes of the lungs show hypertranslucency and hyperinflation. What is her diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The answer is emphysema. Several clues point to it. A low FEV1/FVC ratio means air has trouble getting out of the lungs (an obstructive disease).

A high residual volume and hyperinflated lungs on x-ray mean air is getting trapped. A low diffusion capacity means the gas exchange surface has been destroyed, because emphysema breaks down the walls of the alveoli. Asthma and chronic bronchitis are obstructive too, but they do not usually destroy the alveolar surface.

Big idea: emphysema destroys alveoli, trapping air and reducing gas exchange.

questions.prompt: How will this training change your body’s blood content?
questions.context: You are training for a marathon and your trainer suggests you take your daily runs on top of Stone Mountain. He suggests you go somewhere at high elevation to run.
questions.answer: It will increase RBC, increasing hematocrit
questions.explanation:
Training at high altitude increases the number of red blood cells, which raises the hematocrit (the percent of blood made of red blood cells).

At high altitude, each breath brings in less oxygen. The body responds by making more red blood cells to carry oxygen more efficiently. When the athlete returns to lower altitude, the extra red blood cells can improve endurance.

Big idea: the body adapts to low oxygen by increasing its oxygen-carrying capacity.

questions.prompt: How was a change in blood content caused?
questions.context: You are training for a marathon and your trainer suggests you take your daily runs on top of Stone Mountain. He suggests you go somewhere at high elevation to run.
questions.answer: Low oxygen activates hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which increases production of erythropoietin (EPO), mainly by the kidneys (with a small amount from the liver). EPO tells the bone marrow to make more red blood cells.
questions.officialAnswer: The low oxygen induces release of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) which in turn up-regulates erythropoietin (EPO) production by the liver, which will induce RBC production.
questions.note: The official key says EPO is made by the liver; in adults it is made mainly by the kidneys.
questions.explanation:
Low oxygen levels are sensed by cells, especially in the kidneys, which activate a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). HIF turns on the gene for erythropoietin (EPO).

EPO is a hormone made mainly by the kidneys (with a small amount from the liver). It travels to the bone marrow and tells it to make more red blood cells. (The official key said the liver makes EPO; in adults the kidneys are the main source.)

Big idea: the kidneys sense low oxygen and use EPO to boost red blood cell production.

questions.prompt: A healthy young woman comes into the ER and claims to be experiencing fatigue and nausea since arriving yesterday in your high-altitude city. She has dyspnea while climbing flights of stairs and when walking fast. She asks you if she will be okay if she goes on a hike with her friends. You tell her she will most likely experience this complication.
questions.explanation:
The key's answer is ataxia (loss of coordination). The woman already has signs of acute mountain sickness (fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath) from the low oxygen at high altitude.

If she goes higher or exerts herself before adjusting, mountain sickness can get worse and turn into high-altitude cerebral edema (swelling of the brain). A key early warning sign of this is ataxia: being unsteady and uncoordinated when walking. She should rest and acclimatize first.

Big idea: high altitude lowers oxygen intake, and the body needs time to adjust; pushing too hard can cause serious illness.

questions.prompt: A young boy comes into the ER with a history of recurring pneumonia, chronic coughs, and frequent diarrhea. The physical examination shows a low fever, crepitant rales at the right lung base, and bronchiectasis. The mother is extremely worried and wants you to run tests to find out what her son has. You see signs of a certain disease that affects the respiratory system and decide to run a genetic test on the boy. What will the genetic test show?
questions.answer: mutations in CFTR gene on chromosome 7
questions.explanation:
The genetic test will show mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7, which means the boy has cystic fibrosis.

His clues fit CF: repeated lung infections and pneumonia, chronic cough, and damaged, widened airways (bronchiectasis) from thick, sticky mucus, plus diarrhea because his pancreas cannot release enough enzymes to digest fat. CF is inherited when a child gets two faulty copies of the CFTR gene.

Big idea: CF affects both the respiratory and digestive systems because the faulty CFTR channel makes mucus thick everywhere.

questions.prompt: Where did this infection start in the lungs?
questions.context: A patient is rushed into the ER with a case of bacterial pneumonia. He is in critical condition and an x-ray shows that his left lung has become consolidated.
questions.answer: The infection started in the alveoli
questions.explanation:
Bacterial pneumonia starts in the alveoli. Bacteria reach the alveoli, the tiny air sacs, and multiply there.

The immune response fills the alveoli with fluid, white blood cells, and debris. When a whole area of the lung fills up this way, it becomes solid on an x-ray, which is called consolidation.

Big idea: pneumonia is an infection of the alveoli that fills them with fluid, blocking gas exchange.

questions.prompt: After the onset of this infection, how does the pulmonary membrane change?
questions.context: A patient is rushed into the ER with a case of bacterial pneumonia. He is in critical condition and an x-ray shows that his left lung has become consolidated.
questions.answer: The pulmonary membrane becomes inflamed and highly porous so that fluid and cells leak out of the blood into the alveoli
questions.explanation:
The respiratory membrane becomes inflamed and leaky. Normally this membrane (the thin wall between alveoli and capillaries) keeps blood inside the vessels.

During infection, inflammation makes it highly permeable, so fluid, proteins, red blood cells, and white blood cells leak out of the blood and fill the alveoli. This thickens the barrier and blocks gas exchange, so oxygen levels drop.

Big idea: inflammation helps fight infection, but in the lungs it can flood the alveoli and make breathing hard.

questions.prompt: A patient comes in because of increasing daytime sleepiness. He has been diagnosed with sleep apnea prior to his visit. He has a BMI of 62.6, pulse of 101 bpm, respirations of 13/min, blood pressure of 136/79 mmHg, and normal temperature. His cardiac examination shows no abnormalities. After physically examining him, you note a blue-gray color to his earlobes, nail beds, and lips. The room air arterial blood gas analysis shows a pH of 7.30, PCO2 of 71 mmHg, and PO2 of 51 mmHg. Which additional finding would be most likely in this patient when examining his blood content?
questions.explanation:
The expected finding is increased hemoglobin (more red blood cells, called polycythemia). This patient has severe obesity and sleep apnea, which make his breathing too shallow (hypoventilation).

His blood shows low oxygen (PO2 51) and high carbon dioxide (PCO2 71), and his lips and nails are bluish. Long-term low oxygen makes the kidneys release EPO, which makes the bone marrow produce extra red blood cells to carry more oxygen.

Big idea: chronic low oxygen causes the body to make more red blood cells, just like living at high altitude.

questions.prompt: What can you say about her arterial PO2?
questions.context: A healthy woman frequently enjoys scuba diving. She chooses to dive to a depth of 70 feet in the ocean.
questions.explanation:
Her arterial PO2 will be increased. Underwater, the pressure goes up with depth; at 70 feet it is about three times the pressure at the surface.

Divers breathe air from tanks at the same high pressure as the water around them, so every gas in the air, including oxygen, has a higher partial pressure. More oxygen dissolves into her blood (Henry's Law), raising her arterial PO2.

Big idea: higher pressure pushes more gas into the blood.

questions.prompt: What can you say about her PCO2?
questions.context: A healthy woman frequently enjoys scuba diving. She chooses to dive to a depth of 70 feet in the ocean.
questions.explanation:
Her PCO2 will be about normal. Carbon dioxide in the blood comes from the body's own cells, not from the air (air has almost no CO2).

Her breathing adjusts to remove the CO2 her body makes, so her blood CO2 stays close to normal, even though the oxygen pressure rises.

Big idea: blood CO2 depends on how much the body makes and how much is breathed out, not on the outside pressure.

questions.prompt: A patient has a dead space of 200 milliliters, FRC of 3 liters, VT of 700 milliliters, ERV of 1.5 liters, TLC of 8 liters, and respiratory rate of 17 breaths/min. What is the alveolar ventilation (VA)?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This does not match (700 - 200) x 17.
Incorrect. This does not match (700 - 200) x 17.
Correct. (700 - 200) x 17 = 8500 ml/min = 8.5 L/min.
Incorrect. This does not match (700 - 200) x 17.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 8.5 L/min. Alveolar ventilation is the fresh air that actually reaches the alveoli each minute: (tidal volume - dead space) x breathing rate.

Tidal volume is 700 ml and dead space is 200 ml, so 500 ml of fresh air reaches the alveoli per breath. 500 ml x 17 breaths/min = 8500 ml/min = 8.5 L/min. The FRC, ERV, and TLC are extra information you do not need.

Big idea: dead space air never reaches the alveoli, so subtract it before multiplying by the breathing rate.

questions.prompt: Select ALL structures that can be found in the lower respiratory tract.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The nares (nostrils) are the entrance to the upper respiratory tract.
Incorrect. The pharynx is part of the upper respiratory tract.
Correct. The trachea is the start of the lower respiratory tract.
Correct. Bronchioles are small airways inside the lungs.
Correct. Alveoli are at the very end of the lower respiratory tract.

questions.explanation:
The answers are the trachea, bronchioles, and alveoli. The lower respiratory tract starts at the trachea (some books include the larynx) and goes down through the bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli.

The nares (nostrils) and the pharynx (throat) are part of the upper respiratory tract, which warms, filters, and moistens air before it goes deeper.

Big idea: upper tract = nose, sinuses, pharynx; lower tract = trachea down to the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Gaseous transport through the alveolar membrane is facilitated by which process?

choices.explanation: Correct. O2 and CO2 cross the alveolar membrane by simple diffusion.
Incorrect. Gases do not need protein channels to cross.
Incorrect. Gases do not need carrier proteins.
Incorrect. No energy-using pumps are needed for gas exchange.
Incorrect. Gases are not packaged into vesicles.

questions.explanation:
The answer is simple diffusion. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small molecules that dissolve in the fats of cell membranes, so they pass straight through without any help.

They move from high partial pressure to low partial pressure: oxygen from the alveoli into the blood, and carbon dioxide from the blood into the alveoli. No channels, carrier proteins, pumps, or vesicles are needed, and no energy is used.

Big idea: gas exchange is passive and depends on differences in partial pressure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly matches the anatomical feature to its function?

choices.explanation: Correct. Mucus traps particles from the air you breathe in.

choices.text: Vibrissae; contain a rich supply of capillaries which warm inspired air
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Vibrissae are nose hairs that filter particles; they do not warm air.

choices.text: Glottis; prevents food and drink from entering the trachea when swallowing
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The epiglottis, not the glottis, covers the airway when you swallow.

choices.text: Pleural fluid; prevents gases from leaking out of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pleural fluid reduces friction; it does not keep gases in the lungs.

choices.text: Pharynx; involved in the production of sound
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Sound is produced by the vocal cords in the larynx.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'mucus; traps inhaled particles'. Goblet cells and glands make sticky mucus that catches dust, pollen, and germs. Cilia then sweep the mucus up and out of the airways.

The other matches are wrong. Vibrissae are nose hairs that filter large particles; the rich blood supply that warms air is in the nasal mucosa. The epiglottis (not the glottis, which is the opening between the vocal cords) covers the airway when you swallow. Pleural fluid reduces friction around the lungs. Sound is produced in the larynx, not the pharynx.

Big idea: each part of the respiratory tract has a specific job in cleaning, warming, and moving air.

questions.prompt: Sleep apneas that require medical intervention are typically relieved using which of the following treatments?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inhaled epinephrine is used for emergencies like severe allergic reactions.
Incorrect. Amphetamines are stimulants and do not keep the airway open.
Incorrect. Airway clearance vests loosen mucus, as in cystic fibrosis.
Correct. CPAP keeps the airway open during sleep.
Incorrect. Melatonin helps with falling asleep, not with a blocked airway.

questions.explanation:
The answer is CPAP therapy. CPAP stands for continuous positive airway pressure. A machine gently blows air through a mask while the person sleeps.

In obstructive sleep apnea, the throat relaxes and collapses during sleep, blocking air. The steady air pressure from CPAP holds the airway open like an air splint. The other choices do not treat sleep apnea: epinephrine is for severe allergic reactions, amphetamines are stimulants, airway clearance vests loosen mucus in diseases like cystic fibrosis, and melatonin only helps people fall asleep.

Big idea: sleep apnea is usually caused by a blocked airway, so treatment keeps the airway open.

questions.prompt: CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis are inherited via which inheritance pattern?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. In a dominant disease, one faulty copy would cause it, which is not true for CF.
Correct. CF needs two faulty copies of a gene on a non-sex chromosome.
Incorrect. The CFTR gene is not on the X chromosome.
Incorrect. The CFTR gene is not on the X chromosome.
Incorrect. CF is caused by a single gene, not many genes or mitochondria.

questions.explanation:
The answer is autosomal recessive. The CFTR gene is on chromosome 7, which is an autosome (not a sex chromosome). A person only gets CF if they inherit two faulty copies, one from each parent; that is what 'recessive' means.

People with one faulty copy are carriers. They are healthy but can pass the gene on. If two carriers have a child, there is a 1 in 4 chance the child will have CF.

Big idea: cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

questions.prompt: Identify the structure(s) of the larynx that protrude(s) to form the Adam’s apple.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The ventricular folds are inside the larynx and cannot be seen from outside.
Incorrect. The true vocal cords are inside the larynx.
Incorrect. Tracheal cartilages are the rings below the larynx.
Incorrect. The cricoid cartilage is a ring just below the thyroid cartilage.
Correct. The thyroid cartilage forms the Adam's apple.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the thyroid cartilage. The thyroid cartilage is the largest piece of cartilage in the larynx. Its front edge forms a bump in the neck called the Adam's apple.

The bump gets bigger in males during puberty as the larynx grows. The ventricular folds (false vocal cords) and true vocal cords are inside the larynx. The cricoid cartilage is a ring below the thyroid cartilage, and the tracheal cartilages are the rings of the windpipe.

Big idea: the larynx is built from several cartilages, and the thyroid cartilage is the biggest.

questions.prompt: A pneumothorax occurs as the result of accumulation of air in what structure of the lung?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Air in the bronchioles is normal.
Incorrect. Air in the alveoli is normal.
Correct. A pneumothorax is air in the pleural space.
Incorrect. The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart.
Incorrect. The diaphragm is a muscle, not a space.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pleural space. Each lung is covered by two thin layers of pleura with a small, fluid-filled space between them. Normally this space has no air and a slightly negative pressure, which holds the lung against the chest wall.

In a pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space (from an injury or a burst air pocket). The seal is lost, and the lung collapses. The pericardial cavity surrounds the heart, not the lungs.

Big idea: the lungs stay inflated because the pleural space is sealed.

questions.prompt: Which of the following describes a difference between the right and left lungs?

choices.text: The right lung is made up of two lobes, whereas the left is made up of three
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two.

choices.text: Oblique fissures are found in the right lung, while horizontal fissures are found in the left
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The right lung has both fissures; the left has only an oblique fissure.

choices.text: The left lung is characterized by lingulae and a cardiac notch; no such structures are found in the right lung
choices.explanation: Correct. The lingula and cardiac notch are features of the left lung.

choices.text: There is a greater amount of bronchopulmonary segments in the left lung
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The right lung has more bronchopulmonary segments.

choices.text: A left lung can be transplanted to the right side of the lung cavity, but a right lung cannot be transplanted to the left side
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Each lung is shaped for its own side, so they are not swapped in transplants.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the left lung has a lingula and a cardiac notch, and the right lung does not. Because the heart leans left, the left lung has a dent (the cardiac notch) and a small tongue-shaped flap of its upper lobe (the lingula).

The other statements are wrong. The right lung has three lobes and the left has two. The right lung has both oblique and horizontal fissures, while the left has only an oblique fissure. The right lung has more bronchopulmonary segments. The two lungs are different shapes, so a left lung cannot simply replace a right one.

Big idea: the lungs are not mirror images; the heart shapes the left lung.

questions.prompt: Which of the following represents a sum that equals the total lung capacity?

choices.text: Inspiratory capacity + expiratory reserve volume + residual volume
