questions.explanation:
Label A is the inspiratory reserve volume (IRV). On the spirogram, A is the extra air above a normal breath in, up to the deepest breath you can take.

It is the additional air you can breathe in after a normal breath.

Big idea: the four lung volumes are IRV, tidal volume, ERV, and residual volume.

questions.prompt: What respiratory volume is B referring to? Type out the complete words (do not use abbreviations).
questions.explanation:
Label B is the tidal volume (TV). On the spirogram, B is the height of the small, regular up-and-down waves of quiet breathing.

It is the amount of air moved in or out in one normal breath, about 500 mL.

Big idea: tidal volume is a normal, relaxed breath.

questions.prompt: What respiratory volume is C referring to? Type out the complete words (do not use abbreviations).
questions.explanation:
Label C is the expiratory reserve volume (ERV). On the spirogram, C is the extra air below a normal breath out, down to the hardest breath out.

It is the additional air you can push out after a normal breath out.

Big idea: ERV is the extra air you can force out.

questions.prompt: What respiratory volume is D referring to? Type out the complete words (do not use abbreviations).
questions.explanation:
Label D is the residual volume (RV). On the spirogram, D is the air left at the bottom, below the hardest breath out.

It is the air that always stays in the lungs and keeps the alveoli from collapsing. A spirometer cannot measure it directly.

Big idea: you can never breathe out all the air in your lungs.

questions.prompt: Given the following information, calculate the expiratory reserve volume. Do not include units. Vital Capacity = 4600 mL Inspiratory Capacity = 3500 mL Total Lung Capacity = 5800 mL Tidal Volume = 500 mL
questions.explanation:
The answer is 1100 mL. Vital capacity (VC) = inspiratory capacity (IC) + expiratory reserve volume (ERV).

So ERV = VC - IC = 4600 - 3500 = 1100 mL.

Big idea: use the relationships between volumes and capacities to find a missing value.

questions.prompt: Given the following information, calculate the residual volume. Do not include units. Vital Capacity = 4600 mL Inspiratory Capacity = 3500 mL Total Lung Capacity = 5800 mL Tidal Volume = 500 mL
questions.explanation:
The answer is 1200 mL. Total lung capacity (TLC) = vital capacity (VC) + residual volume (RV).

So RV = TLC - VC = 5800 - 4600 = 1200 mL.

Big idea: residual volume is the part of total lung capacity you cannot breathe out.

questions.prompt: Given the following information, calculate the inspiratory reserve volume. Do not include units. Vital Capacity = 4600 mL Inspiratory Capacity = 3500 mL Total Lung Capacity = 5800 mL Tidal Volume = 500 mL
questions.explanation:
The answer is 3000 mL. Inspiratory capacity (IC) = tidal volume (TV) + inspiratory reserve volume (IRV).

So IRV = IC - TV = 3500 - 500 = 3000 mL.

Big idea: capacities are sums of volumes.

questions.prompt: Label A.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label A is the pharynx (throat), the passage behind the nose and mouth.

Both air and food pass through the pharynx.

Big idea: the pharynx is shared by the respiratory and digestive systems.

questions.prompt: Label B.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label B is the alveoli, the tiny air sacs in the lungs.

Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli.

Big idea: alveoli are the gas exchange surface.

questions.prompt: Label C.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label C is the diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle under the lungs.

The diaphragm contracts and flattens to pull air into the lungs.

Big idea: the diaphragm is the main breathing muscle.

questions.prompt: Label D.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label D is the larynx (voice box), at the top of the trachea in the neck.

The larynx holds the vocal cords and protects the airway during swallowing.

Big idea: the larynx is the voice box and airway guard.

questions.prompt: Label E.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label E is the trachea (windpipe), the tube below the larynx.

Rings of cartilage keep the trachea open as it carries air to the bronchi.

Big idea: the trachea is the main airway into the chest.

questions.prompt: Label F.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label F is the bronchi (one is a bronchus), the large branches of the airway entering each lung.

The trachea splits into the left and right main bronchi, which keep branching inside the lungs.

Big idea: the bronchi carry air into the lungs.

questions.prompt: Label G.
questions.context: Refer to the diagram for questions 58-64.
questions.explanation:
Label G is the bronchioles, the small branching airways inside the lungs.

Bronchioles have no cartilage and use smooth muscle to control their width, carrying air toward the alveoli.

Big idea: bronchioles connect the bronchi to the alveoli.

questions.prompt: What is A?
questions.context: Refer to the diagram of the pharynx for questions 65-67. Identify the three sections.
questions.explanation:
Label A is the nasopharynx, the top part of the pharynx behind the nasal cavity.

Only air passes through the nasopharynx. It contains the adenoids.

Big idea: the pharynx has three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.

questions.prompt: What is B?
questions.context: Refer to the diagram of the pharynx for questions 65-67. Identify the three sections.
questions.explanation:
Label B is the oropharynx, the middle part of the pharynx behind the mouth.

Both air and food pass through it, and it contains the palatine tonsils.

Big idea: the oropharynx is where air and food paths overlap.

questions.prompt: What is C?
questions.context: Refer to the diagram of the pharynx for questions 65-67. Identify the three sections.
questions.explanation:
Label C is the hypopharynx, also called the laryngopharynx, the lowest part of the pharynx.

It lies behind the larynx and leads into both the esophagus and the larynx.

Big idea: the laryngopharynx is where food and air finally separate.

questions.prompt: Aminophylline (theophylline) is prescribed for a client with acute bronchitis. A nurse administers the medication, knowing that the primary action of this medication is to:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Expectorants help bring up mucus; aminophylline is a bronchodilator.
Incorrect. Cough suppressants quiet the cough reflex.

choices.text: Relax smooth muscles of the bronchial airway.
choices.explanation: Correct. Aminophylline relaxes airway smooth muscle.
Incorrect. Antibiotics prevent or treat bacterial infection.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to relax the smooth muscles of the bronchial airways. Aminophylline (a form of theophylline) is a bronchodilator: it widens the airways by relaxing the smooth muscle around them.

Wider airways make breathing easier in conditions like asthma, COPD, and bronchitis. It does not help cough up mucus, suppress coughing, or fight infection.

Big idea: bronchodilators open the airways by relaxing smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: An individual has arterial hypoxemia; PaO2 = 50 mmHg. Which possible cause of this hypoxemia would cause the largest elevation in arterial PCO2?
questions.explanation:
The answer is hypoventilation. Hypoventilation means breathing too little, so not enough fresh air reaches the alveoli.

When you do not breathe enough, oxygen in the blood falls AND carbon dioxide builds up, because CO2 is not being breathed out. Other causes of low oxygen, such as a problem with the alveolar membrane, lower oxygen but usually do not raise CO2 as much, because CO2 diffuses very easily.

Big idea: breathing removes CO2, so breathing too little raises blood CO2.

questions.prompt: The mammalian trachea and esophagus both connect to the ________.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the pharynx. The pharynx (throat) is the shared passage at the back of the nose and mouth.

Below it, the path splits: the larynx and trachea in front for air, and the esophagus behind for food.

Big idea: the pharynx connects to both the respiratory and digestive tracts.

questions.prompt: ___________ is the Increased rate and depth of breathing in response to exercise or pain.
questions.explanation:
The answer is hyperpnea. Hyperpnea means deeper and faster breathing to match a higher need for oxygen, such as during exercise.

It is different from hyperventilation, which is breathing more than the body needs, causing CO2 to drop too low.

Big idea: the body adjusts breathing to match its needs.

questions.prompt: For any partial pressure of oxygen, if the concentration of 2, 3-bisphoglycerate increases the amount of ______ released by hemoglobin will ______
questions.explanation:
The answers are oxygen and increase. 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) is a chemical in red blood cells that binds to hemoglobin and makes it let go of oxygen more easily.

So when 2,3-BPG goes up (for example at high altitude), the amount of oxygen released by hemoglobin at any partial pressure increases. This shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.

Big idea: 2,3-BPG helps hemoglobin deliver more oxygen to the tissues.

questions.prompt: What respiratory disease is a progressive, genetic disease that causes persistent lung infections and limits the ability to breathe over time because of a thick, sticky buildup of mucus in the lungs, pancreas, and other organs.
questions.explanation:
The answer is cystic fibrosis. CF is an inherited disease caused by a faulty CFTR gene. It makes mucus thick and sticky in the lungs, pancreas, and other organs.

In the lungs, the mucus traps bacteria, causing repeated infections and gradually damaging the airways.

Big idea: cystic fibrosis affects both the respiratory and digestive systems.

questions.prompt: The right lung has ___ lobes and the left lung has ___ lobes. (digits)
questions.explanation:
The answers are 3 and 2. The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, and lower), and the left lung has two lobes (upper and lower).

The left lung is smaller because the heart takes up space on the left side.

Big idea: the two lungs are not identical.

questions.prompt: _______also is seen in heart failure. Patients are unable to breathe comfortably, lying flat. They must be in a sitting or propped up to breathe without difficulty
questions.explanation:
The answer is orthopnea. Orthopnea is shortness of breath when lying flat, which improves when sitting or propping up on pillows.

In heart failure, lying down lets fluid shift into the lungs, making breathing harder. Sitting up lets gravity pull the fluid down and away from the lungs.

Big idea: breathing patterns and positions can give clues about disease.

questions.prompt: The ________ muscles are between the ribs that raise and lower the ribs.
questions.explanation:
The answer is intercostal. The intercostal muscles are between the ribs ('inter' = between, 'costal' = ribs).

The external intercostals lift the ribs to help breathe in, and the internal intercostals pull the ribs down during forced breathing out.

Big idea: rib muscles change the size of the chest to help breathing.

questions.prompt: Boyle discovered that the pressure of a gas is _____proportional to its volume at a constant _______
questions.explanation:
The answers are inversely and temperature. Boyle's Law says that at a constant temperature, the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume: when one goes up, the other goes down.

This is how breathing works. When the chest gets bigger, the pressure inside the lungs drops and air flows in.

Big idea: Boyle's Law explains how air moves in and out of the lungs.

questions.prompt: ________' law states that the volume occupied by a gas is directly related to the absolute temperature.
questions.explanation:
The answer is Charles' law. Charles' law says that at a constant pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature: warmer gas takes up more space.

Air warms up as it enters the airways, so it expands a little.

Big idea: different gas laws describe how gases behave in the lungs.

questions.prompt: What is the unit of pulmonary and alveolar ventilation?
questions.explanation:
The answer is liters per minute (L/min). Pulmonary ventilation (total air breathed per minute) and alveolar ventilation (fresh air reaching the alveoli per minute) are both rates.

They are calculated as a volume per breath times breaths per minute, so the units are volume per time, usually L/min (or mL/min).

Big idea: ventilation is a rate of air movement.

questions.prompt: The _______ respiratory group maintains basal tone, controls Tongue Pharynx Larynx and expiratory muscles
questions.explanation:
The answer is ventral. The ventral respiratory group (VRG) in the medulla helps set the breathing rhythm and controls the muscles for forced breathing out, as well as muscles of the tongue, pharynx, and larynx that keep the upper airway open.

The dorsal respiratory group (DRG) mainly controls the muscles for breathing in.

Big idea: different groups of neurons in the brainstem control different parts of breathing.

questions.prompt: What is the bucket handle motion ?
questions.answer: During inspiration- increases lateral dimensions of ribcage
questions.explanation:
The bucket handle motion describes how the lower ribs move when you breathe in. Like the handle of a bucket being lifted, the ribs swing up and out to the sides.

This increases the side-to-side (lateral) width of the rib cage, making the chest bigger so air flows in. (The upper ribs move forward more, like a pump handle.)

Big idea: rib movements enlarge the chest during inspiration.

questions.prompt: Which lung is larger? And why?
questions.answer: The right lung is larger and weighs more than the left lung. Since the heart tilts to the left, the left lung is smaller than the right and has an indentation called the cardiac impression to accommodate the heart.
questions.explanation:
The right lung is larger and heavier than the left lung. The heart tilts to the left, so the left lung has less room.

The left lung has only two lobes and a dent called the cardiac notch where the heart fits.

Big idea: the heart's position shapes the lungs.

questions.prompt: What part of the brain is responsible for ventilatory control ?
questions.answer: 3 defined centers located in the pons and medulla (respiratory centers) -pontine respiratory group (PRG) (pons) -dorsal respiratory group (DRG) (medulla) -ventra respiratory group (VRG) (medulla)
questions.explanation:
Breathing is controlled by respiratory centers in the brainstem: the pons and the medulla. In the medulla, the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) mainly controls breathing in, and the ventral respiratory group (VRG) helps set the rhythm and controls forced breathing.

In the pons, the pontine respiratory group (PRG) smooths out the rhythm and helps switch between breathing in and out.

Big idea: breathing is controlled automatically by the brainstem.

questions.prompt: Altering carbon dioxide production alters the pH. This is a function of the respiratory system.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. Carbon dioxide reacts with water to make carbonic acid, so the amount of CO2 in the blood affects its pH.

By breathing faster or slower, the respiratory system changes how much CO2 is removed, which helps control blood pH.

Big idea: the lungs help regulate blood pH.

questions.prompt: The left lung has both horizontal fissure and oblique fissure.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The left lung has only an oblique fissure, dividing it into two lobes.

The right lung has both a horizontal and an oblique fissure, dividing it into three lobes.

Big idea: the right lung has three lobes and two fissures; the left has two lobes and one fissure.

questions.prompt: The pleural cavities extend two ribs below the inferior border of the lungs.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. The pleural cavity extends about two ribs lower than the bottom edge of the lungs.

This extra space (the costodiaphragmatic recess) lets the lungs expand downward during a deep breath.

Big idea: the pleural cavity is larger than the lungs to give them room to expand.

questions.prompt: The diaphragm is under somatic, voluntary control whereas breathing is under autonomic, involuntary control.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. The diaphragm is skeletal muscle, which can be controlled voluntarily (you can hold your breath or take a deep breath on purpose).

But most of the time, breathing happens automatically, controlled by the brainstem without you thinking about it.

Big idea: breathing has both voluntary and automatic control.

questions.prompt: The vocal ligaments are attached between the cricoid and arytenoid cartilages.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The vocal ligaments (in the vocal cords) stretch between the thyroid cartilage in front and the arytenoid cartilages at the back.

The arytenoids move to tighten or loosen the vocal cords, changing pitch.

Big idea: the vocal cords run from the thyroid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilages.

questions.prompt: In order for inspiration to occur, atmospheric pressure must be greater than intrapulmonary pressure.
questions.note: The official key says False, but air only flows into the lungs when atmospheric pressure is greater than intrapulmonary (alveolar) pressure, so the statement is true.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. For air to flow into the lungs, the pressure outside (atmospheric pressure) must be greater than the pressure inside the lungs (intrapulmonary pressure).

When the diaphragm contracts and the chest expands, intrapulmonary pressure drops below atmospheric pressure, so air flows in. (The official key said False, which is a mistake.)

Big idea: air flows from higher pressure to lower pressure.

questions.prompt: Type I cells produce surfactant.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. Type II alveolar cells make surfactant.

Type I cells are thin, flat cells that form most of the alveolar wall and allow fast gas exchange.

Big idea: type I = gas exchange; type II = surfactant.

questions.prompt: Palatine tonsil, pharyngeal tonsil and tubal tonsil are all located within the nasopharynx.
questions.explanation:
This statement is false. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) and the tubal tonsils are in the nasopharynx, but the palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx.

Big idea: different tonsils guard different parts of the throat.

questions.prompt: Stimulation of the stretch receptors in the lungs prevents over inflation of the lungs.
questions.explanation:
This statement is true. Stretch receptors in the walls of the airways sense when the lungs are filling with air.

When the lungs stretch a lot, these receptors send signals through the vagus nerve that stop inhalation. This is the Hering-Breuer reflex, which protects the lungs from over-inflating.

Big idea: reflexes protect the lungs.

questions.prompt: Smallest airway that is primarily responsible for creating bronchoconstriction.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Incorrect. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Incorrect. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Correct. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the bronchiole. Bronchioles have smooth muscle and no cartilage, so when this muscle tightens (bronchoconstriction), they narrow a lot, as in asthma.

Big idea: bronchioles control airflow with smooth muscle.

questions.prompt: Alveolar cells that allow rapid diffusion of respiratory gases.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Incorrect. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Correct. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Incorrect. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is type I alveolar cells. These are very thin, flat cells that make up most of the alveolar wall, so gases can diffuse across them quickly.

Big idea: thin type I cells allow fast gas exchange.

questions.prompt: The serous membrane lining of the wall of the thoracic cavity.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Correct. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Incorrect. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Incorrect. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Incorrect. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the parietal pleura. The parietal pleura lines the inner wall of the chest cavity, the diaphragm, and the mediastinum.

Big idea: parietal = wall; visceral = organ.

questions.prompt: The region of the lung served by secondary, or lobar, bronchi.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Incorrect. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Correct. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Incorrect. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Incorrect. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is a lobe. Each lobe of a lung is supplied by its own secondary (lobar) bronchus: three on the right and two on the left.

Big idea: lobes match the secondary bronchi.

questions.prompt: Fluid that reduces surface tension of the alveolar walls.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Correct. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Incorrect. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Incorrect. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is surfactant. Surfactant lowers the surface tension of the water lining the alveoli, keeping them from collapsing.

Big idea: surfactant keeps alveoli open.

questions.prompt: Subdivision of the lungs in which gas exchange occurs.
questions.context: Match the following:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Parietal pleura: the serous membrane lining the wall of the chest cavity.
Incorrect. Surfactant: the fluid that reduces surface tension in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Lobe: the region of lung served by a secondary (lobar) bronchus.
Incorrect. Type I cells: thin alveolar cells that allow fast gas diffusion.
Incorrect. Bronchiole: small airway whose smooth muscle causes bronchoconstriction.
Correct. Alveoli: the tiny air sacs where gas exchange occurs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the alveoli. The alveoli are the tiny air sacs where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

Big idea: gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.prompt: With respect to normal exhalation, what is the proper sequence of the following events? (enter the letters only, separated by commas) A. Motor impulses from the medulla decrease. B. The chest cavity becomes smaller, and the elastic connective tissue around the alveoli recoils. C. Intrapulmonic pressure rises above atmospheric pressure. D. The lungs are compressed. E. The diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax. F. Air is forced out of the lungs until intrapulmonic pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
answer: A, E, B, D, C, F
officialAnswer: A, C, E, D, B, F
questions.note: The official key gives A, C, E, D, B, F, which puts the pressure rise (C) before the muscles relax; the physiological order is A, E, B, D, C, F.
questions.explanation:
The correct order is A, E, B, D, C, F. First, the medulla stops sending signals to the breathing muscles (A). Then the diaphragm and external intercostals relax (E).

The chest cavity gets smaller and the elastic tissue in the lungs recoils (B), which squeezes the lungs (D). This raises the pressure in the lungs above atmospheric pressure (C), so air flows out until the pressures are equal (F). (The official key listed A, C, E, D, B, F, which puts the pressure rise before the muscles relax.)

Big idea: normal breathing out is passive: muscles relax, the chest shrinks, pressure rises, and air flows out.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statement indicate the correct partial pressure for each gas in each site?
questions.context: The following diagram depicts one alveolus and a pulmonary capillary. Use this diagram to answer questions 104 through 106. The presence of each respiratory gas in each site is shown, indicated as PO2 or PCO2.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Site 3 (alveolar air) should be low in CO2, and site 4 (blood) high.
Incorrect. Site 1 (alveolar air) should be high in O2.
Correct. Alveolar air: high O2, low CO2; capillary blood arriving: low O2, high CO2.
Incorrect. Site 1 (alveolar air) should be high in O2.

questions.explanation:
The answer is C. Air in the alveolus (site 1) has high oxygen, while blood arriving in the capillary (site 2) has low oxygen, so oxygen moves into the blood.

Blood arriving at the lungs is high in carbon dioxide (site 4), while the alveolar air is lower in CO2 (site 3), so CO2 moves out of the blood into the alveolus. Gases always diffuse from high to low partial pressure.

Big idea: oxygen moves into the blood and CO2 moves out, each down its own gradient.

questions.prompt: This exchange of gases is called __________respiration.
questions.context: The following diagram depicts one alveolus and a pulmonary capillary. Use this diagram to answer questions 104 through 106. The presence of each respiratory gas in each site is shown, indicated as PO2 or PCO2.

choices.explanation: Correct. Gas exchange between alveoli and blood is external respiration.
Incorrect. Internal respiration happens at the body's tissues.
Incorrect. This is not a type of respiration.
Incorrect. This is not a type of respiration.

questions.explanation:
The answer is external respiration. External respiration is gas exchange between the alveoli and the blood in the lungs.

Internal respiration is gas exchange between the blood and the body's tissues.

Big idea: external = lungs; internal = tissues.

questions.prompt: Coughing will cause the trachealis muscle to

choices.text: contract which will narrow the diameter of the trachea.
choices.explanation: Correct. The trachealis contracts and narrows the trachea, speeding airflow during a cough.

choices.text: relax which will increase the diameter of the trachea.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The trachealis contracts during a cough, not relaxes.

choices.text: contract which will close the false vocal cords.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The trachealis does not control the false vocal cords.

choices.text: relax, which will open the false vocal cords.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The trachealis does not control the false vocal cords.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the trachealis muscle contracts, narrowing the trachea. The trachealis is smooth muscle at the back of the trachea, across the open part of the C-shaped cartilage rings.

During a cough, it contracts, making the trachea narrower. This speeds up the air rushing out, helping blast mucus and debris out of the airway.

Big idea: narrowing a tube speeds up the air flowing through it.

questions.prompt: Pleural fluid helps keep the _______ expanded against the _______ walls.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pleural fluid holds the lungs, not the diaphragm.
Incorrect. The trachea is not inside the pleural cavity.
Incorrect. The bronchi are inside the lungs, not directly against the chest wall.
Correct. Pleural fluid keeps the lungs expanded against the thoracic walls.

questions.explanation:
The answer is lungs, thoracic. Pleural fluid creates surface tension between the two pleural layers, holding the lungs against the thoracic (chest) wall.

This keeps the lungs expanded, so they move outward with the chest wall when you breathe in.

Big idea: pleural fluid holds the lungs to the chest wall.

questions.prompt: If the elastic fibers were removed from around the alveolar sacs, the lungs in normal breathing would lose most of their ability to

choices.text: expand so inhalation would be impeded.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Expansion depends on the muscles, not the elastic fibers.

choices.text: expand so exhalation would be impeded.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Exhalation depends on recoil, not expansion.

choices.text: recoil so exhalation would be impeded.
choices.explanation: Correct. Without elastic recoil, breathing out would be impeded.

choices.text: recoil so inhalation would be impeded.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Recoil drives exhalation, not inhalation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the lungs would lose their ability to recoil, so exhalation would be impeded. Normal, quiet breathing out is passive: the stretched elastic fibers spring back, pushing air out.

Without elastic fibers, the lungs could still be expanded by the chest muscles, but they would not spring back on their own. This loss of recoil is what happens in emphysema.

Big idea: elastic recoil powers normal breathing out.

questions.prompt: The left lung is _____ than the right lung and is divided into ___ lobes.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The left lung is smaller, not larger.
Incorrect. The left lung is smaller and has two lobes.
Correct. The left lung is smaller and has two lobes.
Incorrect. The left lung has two lobes, not three.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'smaller; 2'. The left lung is smaller than the right because the heart takes up space on the left.

It has two lobes; the right lung has three.

Big idea: the heart makes the left lung smaller.

questions.prompt: Breathing is controlled by the chemistry of your blood as it interacts with the

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The cerebrum handles thinking and voluntary control.
Incorrect. The cerebellum coordinates movement and balance.
Incorrect. The hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, and hormones.
Correct. The medulla oblongata controls breathing.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the medulla oblongata. The medulla, in the brainstem, contains the main breathing centers.

It responds to the chemistry of the blood (CO2, O2, and pH) and adjusts the rate and depth of breathing.

Big idea: the medulla is the breathing control center.

questions.prompt: In the alveoli, an exchange of gases take place within the capillaries of the lungs. Which of the following is the correct gas exchange?

choices.text: Carbon dioxide leaves the capillaries because there is a high concentration of carbon dioxide in the air of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. CO2 leaves the capillaries because it is higher in the blood, not in the air.

choices.text: Carbon dioxide enters the capillaries because there is a high concentration of oxygen in the air of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. CO2 leaves the capillaries; it does not enter them.

choices.text: Oxygen leaves the capillaries because there is a high concentration of oxygen in the air of the lungs
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Oxygen enters the capillaries; it does not leave them in the lungs.

choices.text: Oxygen enters the capillaries because there is a high concentration of oxygen in the air of the lungs
choices.explanation: Correct. Oxygen diffuses into the capillaries from the oxygen-rich alveolar air.

questions.explanation:
The answer is D: oxygen enters the capillaries because there is a high concentration of oxygen in the air of the lungs. Gases diffuse from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated.

Oxygen is higher in the alveolar air, so it moves into the blood. Carbon dioxide is higher in the blood, so it moves out of the capillaries into the alveoli; it does not enter them.

Big idea: each gas diffuses down its own concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Tuberculosis is an infection caused by a

choices.explanation: Incorrect. TB is not caused by a virus.
Incorrect. TB is not caused by a fungus.
Correct. TB is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
Incorrect. Prions cause brain diseases, not TB.

questions.explanation:
The answer is bacteria. Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

It spreads through the air and mainly infects the lungs. It is treated with several antibiotics taken for months.

Big idea: TB is a bacterial lung infection.

questions.prompt: 23% of carbon dioxide is transported in red blood cells as

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Oxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin carrying oxygen.
Official answer, but mislabeled. The right term is carbaminohemoglobin; carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide.
Incorrect. Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas, not a way CO2 is carried.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate carries about 70% of CO2, mostly in the plasma.

questions.note: Uncertain: about 23% of CO2 rides on hemoglobin as carbaminohemoglobin, which is not offered; the official key picks "carboxyhemoglobin", which is actually hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide.
questions.explanation:
The intended answer is carbaminohemoglobin, which is not listed. About 23% of carbon dioxide travels bound to the protein part of hemoglobin, forming carbaminohemoglobin.

The official key chose 'carboxyhemoglobin', but that word actually means hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide (CO), which is poisonous. The names are easy to confuse. Most CO2 (about 70%) travels as bicarbonate, but that is mostly in the plasma.

Big idea: CO2 travels as bicarbonate, as carbaminohemoglobin, and dissolved in plasma.

questions.prompt: What is the function of surfactant in the lungs?

choices.text: Coat the lungs to allow smooth transfer of gases.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Surfactant does not directly move gases.

choices.text: Lower the surface tension at the air/liquid interface within the alveoli.
choices.explanation: Correct. Surfactant lowers surface tension in the alveoli.

choices.text: Used for increases the volume of air during inhalation.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Surfactant does not directly increase air volume.

choices.text: Covers the bronchial airways to support nutrient passage.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Surfactant does not deliver nutrients.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to lower the surface tension at the air/liquid interface within the alveoli. Surfactant keeps the alveoli from collapsing and makes breathing easier.

It does not directly transfer gases, increase air volume, or deliver nutrients.

Big idea: surfactant reduces surface tension in the alveoli.

questions.prompt: If pH decreases, PCO2 increases, or temperature increases, the amount of oxygen bound to hemoglobin

choices.explanation: Incorrect. These conditions make hemoglobin release oxygen, not hold more.
Correct. Hemoglobin releases oxygen, so less stays bound.
Incorrect. These conditions do change hemoglobin's binding.
Incorrect. The effect is well known: binding decreases.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the amount of oxygen bound to hemoglobin decreases. Lower pH (more acid), more CO2, and higher temperature all make hemoglobin let go of oxygen.

This shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right (the Bohr effect), delivering more oxygen to active tissues.

Big idea: active tissues are warm, acidic, and high in CO2, so they get more oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which of the following physiological changes are you likely to experience during the first few days at high altitude?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pulse rate goes up at high altitude.
Correct. Blood pressure rises in the first few days at high altitude.
Incorrect. Appetite usually decreases at high altitude.
Incorrect. Only increased blood pressure is correct.

questions.explanation:
The answer is increased blood pressure. In the first few days at high altitude, the low oxygen activates the sympathetic nervous system.

Heart rate and blood pressure go up, and appetite usually goes down. So 'decreased pulse rate' and 'increased appetite' are wrong.

Big idea: the body responds quickly to low oxygen by working harder.

questions.prompt: The carina marks the point where the ________branches into the two main ________.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The bronchi branch into bronchioles deeper in the lungs.
Incorrect. The carina is not in the nose.
Correct. The trachea splits into the two main bronchi at the carina.
Incorrect. The carina is not where alveoli begin.

questions.explanation:
The answer is trachea, bronchi. The carina is a ridge of cartilage where the trachea splits into the left and right main bronchi.

It is very sensitive, so anything touching it triggers a strong cough.

Big idea: the carina marks where the airway branches.

questions.prompt: What determines whether carbon dioxide is absorbed or released by blood?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Capillary size does not decide the direction of CO2 movement.
Incorrect. Total air pressure does not decide this; the CO2 gradient does.
Incorrect. Hemoglobin affects how much CO2 is carried, not the direction.
Correct. Concentration gradients decide whether CO2 is picked up or released.

questions.explanation:
The answer is concentration gradients. Carbon dioxide moves by diffusion from where its partial pressure (concentration) is higher to where it is lower.

In the tissues, CO2 is higher in the cells, so blood picks it up. In the lungs, CO2 is higher in the blood, so it is released into the alveoli.

Big idea: gradients drive gas exchange.

questions.prompt: Pneumothorax is the introduction of air into the pleural cavity through an opening resulting from penetration trauma, such as that caused by a knife. As a result of air in the pleural cavity the lungs tend to

choices.text: be less elastic and you cannot exhale.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The lungs do not lose elasticity; they collapse because of it.
Correct. Air in the pleural cavity lets the lung collapse.
Incorrect. The lungs collapse; they do not over-inflate.

choices.text: increase the surface tension in the fluid lining the alveoli.
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Pneumothorax does not affect surface tension in the alveoli.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the lungs tend to collapse. Normally the pleural cavity is sealed with slightly negative pressure, which holds the lungs open against the chest wall.

When air enters the pleural cavity (pneumothorax), the seal is lost, and the lung's own elastic recoil makes it collapse.

Big idea: the sealed pleural cavity keeps the lungs inflated.

questions.prompt: What is the deficiency of oxygen in the blood (usually a sign of respiratory impairment) called?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease, not the name for low blood oxygen.
Incorrect. Epistaxis is a nosebleed.
Incorrect. Emphysema is a disease that can cause low oxygen, not the name for it.
Correct. Hypoxemia is a deficiency of oxygen in the blood.

questions.explanation:
The answer is hypoxemia, meaning low oxygen in the blood. It is often a sign of lung disease.

Cystic fibrosis and emphysema are diseases that can cause hypoxemia, and epistaxis means a nosebleed.

Big idea: hypoxemia = low blood oxygen; hypoxia = low tissue oxygen.

questions.prompt: What gas is found in the greatest quantity in exhaled air?
questions.explanation:
The answer is nitrogen. Air is about 78% nitrogen, and the body does not use it, so it is breathed out unchanged.

Exhaled air still contains much more nitrogen than oxygen (about 16%) or carbon dioxide (about 4%).

Big idea: we only exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide; nitrogen just passes through.

questions.prompt: The volume of air in a normal breath is called __________ volume.
questions.explanation:
The answer is tidal volume. Tidal volume is the amount of air moved in or out with a normal, quiet breath, about 500 mL in adults.

Big idea: tidal volume is a normal breath.

questions.prompt: How thick are the walls of the alveoli?
questions.explanation:
The answer is one cell thick. The alveolar walls are made of a single layer of thin, flat type I cells.

This makes the distance for gas diffusion very short.

Big idea: thin walls make gas exchange fast.

questions.prompt: When the _______ muscles contract, the size of the thoracic cavity increases in both length and diameter.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the inspiratory muscles. The diaphragm (which makes the chest longer) and external intercostals (which make it wider) are the main inspiratory muscles.

When they contract, the chest gets bigger and air flows in.

Big idea: inspiratory muscles enlarge the chest.

questions.prompt: What three laws describe the properties of gas exchange in the lungs? ______ law, _____ law and _____ law (ENTER ALPHABETICALLY)
questions.explanation:
The answers are Boyle's law, Dalton's law, and Henry's law. Boyle's law explains how changing lung volume changes pressure, which moves air in and out.

Dalton's law explains partial pressures of each gas in air. Henry's law explains how gases dissolve into the blood based on their partial pressures.

Big idea: gas laws explain breathing and gas exchange.

questions.prompt: The volume is the volume of air inspired in a regular breath.
questions.explanation:
The answer is tidal volume, the volume of air breathed in or out during a regular, relaxed breath.

Big idea: tidal volume is a normal breath.

questions.prompt: Breathing is usually regulated by CO2 and O2 ________ and __-level sensors
questions.explanation:
The answers are concentration and pH. Breathing is controlled by chemoreceptors that sense the concentrations of carbon dioxide and oxygen in the blood, and the blood's pH.

Rising CO2 or falling pH makes you breathe faster and deeper.

Big idea: blood chemistry controls breathing.

questions.prompt: ______ is the term for labored, gasping shortness of breath.
questions.explanation:
The answer is dyspnea. Dyspnea means difficult or labored breathing, the feeling of being short of breath.

Big idea: dyspnea is a symptom of many lung and heart diseases.

questions.prompt: The presence of an abnormally low carbon dioxide content in the blood is known as ___________.
questions.explanation:
The answer is hypocapnia. 'Hypo' means low, and 'capnia' refers to carbon dioxide.

It is usually caused by breathing too fast (hyperventilation), which blows off too much CO2.

Big idea: breathing rate controls blood CO2.

questions.prompt: In tissues at a normal partial pressure of oxygen, blood entering the venous system contains about _____% of its total oxygen content. (integer)
questions.explanation:
The answer is about 75%. At rest, blood gives up only about a quarter of its oxygen to the tissues.

So blood entering the veins is still about 75% saturated. This leftover oxygen is a reserve the body can use during exercise.

Big idea: the body keeps an oxygen reserve in venous blood.

questions.prompt: The apneustic centers of the pons inhibit the ______ and _______ centers. (ENTER ALPHABETICALLY)
questions.note: Uncertain: in standard physiology the apneustic center stimulates (prolongs) inspiration and is itself inhibited by the pneumotaxic center and lung stretch receptors, so the statement in this question does not match textbooks.
questions.explanation:
The key's answers are inspiratory and pneumotaxic, but this question is uncertain. In standard textbooks, the apneustic center in the pons actually stimulates the inspiratory center, making breaths in longer and deeper.

The apneustic center is itself inhibited by the pneumotaxic center and by stretch receptors in the lungs. When the pneumotaxic center is damaged, the apneustic center causes long, gasping breaths in (apneustic breathing).

Big idea: the pons fine-tunes the breathing rhythm set by the medulla.

questions.prompt: Surfactant produced by cells lining the alveoli serves to reduce ______ of water molecules
questions.explanation:
The answer is cohesion. Water molecules strongly attract each other (cohesion), which creates surface tension in the thin water layer lining the alveoli.

Surfactant gets between the water molecules and reduces this attraction, which lowers surface tension and keeps the alveoli from collapsing.

Big idea: surfactant makes the lungs easier to inflate.

questions.prompt: The air pressure at the top of Mt. Everest is about 1/3 of the air pressure in Gainesville, FL. What is the partial pressure of O2 at the top of Mt. Everest? _____ atm (decimal)
questions.explanation:
The answer is about 0.07 atm. At sea level, total air pressure is about 1 atm, and oxygen is 21% of air, so its partial pressure is about 0.21 atm.

At the top of Everest, total pressure is about 1/3 atm. Oxygen is still 21%, so 0.21 x 1/3 is about 0.07 atm (Dalton's Law).

Big idea: partial pressure = fraction of the gas x total pressure.

questions.prompt: The function of the respiratory tract _______ is to move dirty mucus toward the throat to be swallowed.
questions.explanation:
The answer is cilia. Cilia on the airway lining beat in coordinated waves, moving mucus (and trapped dust and germs) up toward the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out.

This is called the mucociliary escalator.

Big idea: mucus and cilia protect the lungs.

questions.prompt: A condition caused by excess fluid in the lungs, which collects in the numerous air sacs in the lungs, making it difficult to breathe is known as Pulmonary _______
questions.explanation:
The answer is pulmonary edema. Edema means swelling from extra fluid.

In pulmonary edema, fluid leaks into the alveoli, often because of heart failure, which blocks gas exchange and makes breathing hard.

Big idea: fluid in the alveoli prevents gas exchange.

questions.prompt: The vestibule of the nasal cavity is lined with stratified _______epithelium
questions.explanation:
The answer is squamous (stratified squamous epithelium). The vestibule is the area just inside the nostrils.

It is lined with skin-like stratified squamous epithelium with nose hairs, which is tough and protects against rubbing. Deeper in, the lining changes to ciliated respiratory epithelium.

Big idea: the lining of the airway changes to match each region's job.

questions.prompt: The erectile tissue in the Inferior ___________ periodically restricts airflow through one fossa.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the inferior concha. The nasal conchae are curved bony shelves in the nasal cavity covered by mucous membrane.

The inferior conchae have erectile tissue that swells and shrinks, taking turns on each side. This 'nasal cycle' lets one side rest while the other does most of the breathing.

Big idea: the nose warms, moistens, and filters air.

questions.prompt: What test can be used to diagnose COPD?
questions.explanation:
The answer is spirometry. Spirometry measures how much and how fast a person can breathe out.

In COPD, the amount blown out in the first second (FEV1) is low compared to the total (FVC), showing that airflow is obstructed.

Big idea: spirometry diagnoses obstructive lung diseases like COPD.

questions.prompt: ____________ (chemical name) describes the way 60% of carbon dioxide is transported in blood
questions.explanation:
The answer is bicarbonate. Most carbon dioxide (about 60-70%) is carried in the blood as bicarbonate ions (HCO3-).

Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells turns CO2 and water into carbonic acid, which splits into bicarbonate and hydrogen ions.

Big idea: CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate.

questions.prompt: What structure covers the immediate surface of the lungs?
questions.explanation:
The answer is the visceral pleura. The visceral pleura is a thin membrane that covers the surface of each lung and dips into its fissures.

Big idea: visceral = on the organ; parietal = on the wall.

questions.prompt: ______breathing is another abnormal breathing pattern. It results from injury to the upper pons by a stroke or trauma. It is characterized by regular deep inspirations with an inspiratory pause followed by inadequate expiration.
questions.explanation:
The answer is apneustic breathing. When the upper pons (the pneumotaxic center) is damaged, the inspiratory 'off switch' is lost.

The person takes long, deep breaths in with a pause at the top and short, inadequate breaths out.

Big idea: damage to breathing centers causes recognizable abnormal patterns.

questions.prompt: _____respiratory pattern is characterized by regular deep respirations interspersed with periods of apnea. It is caused by damage to the pons due to stroke, trauma, or uncal herniation
questions.explanation:
The answer is Biot breathing. Biot breathing has groups of deep breaths of about the same size, separated by pauses (apnea).

It is caused by damage to the pons or medulla from stroke, trauma, or brain herniation.

Big idea: Biot = clusters of breaths with pauses.

questions.prompt: _____ - ______ respiration is a pattern of crescendo-decrescendo respirations followed by a period of apnea.
questions.explanation:
The answer is Cheyne-Stokes respiration. Breaths gradually get deeper, then shallower (crescendo-decrescendo), followed by a pause with no breathing, and the cycle repeats.

It is often seen in heart failure, stroke, or at high altitude during sleep.

Big idea: Cheyne-Stokes = waxing and waning breaths with pauses.

questions.prompt: The ________cells and the ______ glands are associated with mucous?
questions.explanation:
The answers are goblet cells and subepithelial (submucosal) glands. Goblet cells in the airway lining and glands beneath the lining both produce mucus.

The mucus traps dust and germs, and cilia sweep it away.

Big idea: mucus is made by goblet cells and submucosal glands.

questions.prompt: What is each cluster of alveoli surrounded by ____ fibers and a network of ______
questions.explanation:
The answers are elastic fibers and capillaries. Each cluster of alveoli is wrapped in elastic fibers, which let the lungs stretch when you breathe in and spring back when you breathe out.

It is also surrounded by a dense network of capillaries for gas exchange.

Big idea: elastic fibers provide recoil; capillaries provide gas exchange.

questions.prompt: What air passages don't contain C - shaped rings of cartilage?
questions.explanation:
The answer is bronchioles. The trachea and bronchi are held open by cartilage.

Bronchioles have no cartilage; instead they have smooth muscle that controls their width.

Big idea: cartilage decreases and smooth muscle increases as airways get smaller.

questions.prompt: Both pleural membranes closely connected by ________ forces of the ________ fluid
questions.explanation:
The answers are cohesive and pleural. The two pleural membranes are held tightly together by the surface tension (cohesive forces) of the thin layer of pleural fluid between them, like two wet glass slides stuck together.

This keeps the lungs stuck to the chest wall so they expand when the chest expands.

Big idea: pleural fluid both lubricates and holds the lungs to the chest wall.

questions.prompt: _________ ________ capacity is the volume of air that is in our lungs at the end of normal expiration ERV + RV
questions.explanation:
The answer is functional residual capacity (FRC). FRC is the air left in the lungs after a normal breath out.

It equals the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume.

Big idea: FRC = ERV + RV.

questions.prompt: ________ capacity is the volume breathed in from quiet expiration to maximum inspiration TV + IRV.
questions.explanation:
The answer is inspiratory capacity. Inspiratory capacity is the most air you can breathe in, starting from a normal breath out.

It equals the tidal volume plus the inspiratory reserve volume.

Big idea: IC = TV + IRV.

questions.prompt: The external ______ muscles are involved in normal inspiration.
questions.explanation:
The answer is intercostal (the external intercostal muscles). These muscles between the ribs lift the ribs up and out during normal breathing in.

Big idea: the diaphragm and external intercostals drive quiet inspiration.

questions.prompt: During the inspiratory phase the alveolar pressure is always less than __________ pressure.
questions.explanation:
The answer is atmospheric pressure. During inspiration, the chest expands and the pressure in the alveoli drops below the air pressure outside the body.

That pressure difference is what makes air flow in.

Big idea: air flows from high pressure to low pressure.

questions.prompt: The intrapleural pressure during inspiration becomes more __________.
questions.explanation:
The answer is negative. The pressure in the pleural space is always slightly below atmospheric pressure.

When you breathe in and the chest expands, the intrapleural pressure becomes even more negative, pulling the lungs open.

Big idea: negative pleural pressure keeps the lungs inflated.

questions.prompt: The respiratory disorder __________is characterized by Inert fibrous tissue means effort of inspiration increases and decreases compliance of the lungs
questions.explanation:
The answer is (pulmonary) fibrosis. In pulmonary fibrosis, lung tissue is replaced by stiff scar tissue.

Stiff lungs are hard to stretch (low compliance), so breathing in takes much more effort. It is a restrictive lung disease.

Big idea: scarred lungs are stiff and hard to inflate.

questions.prompt: Surfactant production stimulated by ______ (organ) hormones and ________ hormone produced by the adrenal gland.
questions.explanation:
The answers are thyroid and cortisol. Hormones from the thyroid gland and cortisol from the adrenal gland help the lungs mature and make surfactant.

That is why steroids are given to mothers expecting a premature baby, to boost the baby's surfactant.

Big idea: hormones help lungs mature before birth.

questions.prompt: The ______ respiratory group controls Inspiratory muscles, via phrenic and intercostal nerve.
questions.explanation:
The answer is the dorsal respiratory group (DRG). The DRG in the medulla mainly controls the inspiratory muscles.

It sends signals through the phrenic nerve to the diaphragm and through the intercostal nerves to the rib muscles.

Big idea: the DRG controls breathing in.

questions.prompt: The respiratory process consists of 3 components: (ENTER ALPHABETICALLY)
questions.explanation:
The answers are diffusion, perfusion, and ventilation. Ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs. Diffusion is gases crossing between the alveoli and the blood.

Perfusion is blood flowing through the lung capillaries to carry gases away. All three are needed for respiration.

Big idea: good gas exchange needs air (ventilation), blood (perfusion), and diffusion between them.

questions.prompt: What happens to PO2 and PCO2 during hyperventilation?
questions.answer: -PO2 rises to about 120mmHg -PCO2 falls to about 20 mmHg
questions.explanation:
During hyperventilation, you breathe faster and deeper than needed. More fresh air reaches the alveoli, so the oxygen level (PO2) rises, to about 120 mmHg.

Much more CO2 is blown off, so the CO2 level (PCO2) falls, to about 20 mmHg. Low CO2 makes the blood more basic and can cause dizziness and tingling.

Big idea: breathing more lowers blood CO2 much more than it raises O2.

questions.prompt: What force needs to be overcome during inspiration ?
questions.answer: Inward force caused by the elasticity of the lungs - they are stretched slightly open even at the end of a relaxed expiration - natural tendency to recoil (contract inwards)
questions.explanation:
During inspiration, you must overcome the lungs' natural inward pull. The lungs are stretchy, like a balloon, and their elastic fibers (plus surface tension in the alveoli) always try to pull them back to a smaller size.

Even at the end of a relaxed breath out, the lungs are still stretched a little, so the breathing muscles must work against this recoil to expand them.

Big idea: the lungs naturally want to recoil inward; breathing in takes work against that.

questions.prompt: Describe type 2 Pneumocytes
questions.answer: Surfactant production Phospholipids and protein Reduces surface tension at alveolar surface Reduces work of breathing
questions.explanation:
Type II pneumocytes are rounded cells in the alveolar walls. Their main job is to make surfactant, a mix of phospholipids (fats) and proteins.

Surfactant reduces surface tension at the alveolar surface, which keeps the alveoli from collapsing and reduces the work of breathing. Type II cells can also divide to replace damaged type I cells.

Big idea: type II cells keep the alveoli open and repaired.

questions.prompt: What is the function of conducting airways and why?
questions.answer: The walls of the upper airways are too thick to allow gasses to cross and their function is purely conduction of air to and from the alveoli (the air in these airways i known as anatomical dead space because it cannot participate in gas exchange).
questions.explanation:
The conducting airways (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles) only move air to and from the alveoli, while warming, moistening, and filtering it.

Their walls are too thick for gases to cross, so no gas exchange happens there. The air in them is called anatomical dead space, because it never takes part in gas exchange.

Big idea: conducting airways move air; only the respiratory zone exchanges gases.

questions.prompt: Explain why the C-rings of the trachea are incomplete.
questions.answer: allow the trachea to collapse slightly to allow food to pass down the esophagus
questions.explanation:
The C-shaped cartilage rings of the trachea are open at the back, where the trachea touches the esophagus.

The open part is covered by soft muscle (the trachealis). This lets the esophagus bulge forward into the trachea's space when a large bite of food is swallowed. The rings still keep the trachea open for breathing.

Big idea: the trachea's shape balances keeping the airway open with letting food pass behind it.

questions.prompt: The right lung has __ lobes and the left lung has __ lobes

choices.explanation: Correct. Right lung: 3 lobes; left lung: 2 lobes.
Incorrect. This reverses the lungs.
Incorrect. The left lung has only two lobes.
Incorrect. The right lung has three lobes.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 3, 2. The right lung has three lobes (upper, middle, and lower). The left lung has two (upper and lower), because the heart takes up space on the left.

Big idea: the lungs are not identical; the heart makes the left lung smaller.

questions.prompt: During Expiration:

choices.text: the thoracic cavity increases in volume
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The thoracic cavity decreases in volume during expiration.
Correct. The diaphragm relaxes during expiration.
Incorrect. Air flows out of the lungs during expiration.
Incorrect. Only B is true for expiration.

questions.explanation:
The answer is that the diaphragm relaxes. During expiration (breathing out), the diaphragm relaxes and moves back up into its dome shape.

This makes the chest smaller, raising the pressure in the lungs so air flows out. The chest does not get bigger, and air flows out, not in.

Big idea: relaxing the diaphragm shrinks the chest and pushes air out.

questions.prompt: The exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs in the:

choices.explanation: Correct. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.
Incorrect. Bronchi carry air.
Incorrect. Most bronchioles only carry air.
Incorrect. The pleura surrounds the lungs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the alveoli, the tiny air sacs whose thin walls let oxygen move into the blood and carbon dioxide move out.

The bronchi and bronchioles carry air, and the pleura is the membrane around the lungs.

Big idea: gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.prompt: During inspiration:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Intra-alveolar pressure decreases during inspiration.
Incorrect by itself. True, but C is also true.
Incorrect by itself. True, but B is also true.

choices.text: Both b and c are correct
choices.explanation: Correct. Both intra-alveolar and intrapleural pressure decrease.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'Both b and c are correct'. When you breathe in, the chest expands. The pressure inside the alveoli (intra-alveolar pressure) drops below the outside air pressure, so air flows in.

The pressure in the pleural space around the lungs (intrapleural pressure) also becomes more negative, which helps pull the lungs open.

Big idea: breathing in lowers the pressures inside the chest.

questions.prompt: What is the function of the bronchioles

choices.text: transport blood and nutrients to cells in the body
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Blood vessels carry blood and nutrients.

choices.text: facilitate the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The alveoli exchange gases.
Correct. Bronchioles carry air to the alveoli.
Incorrect. The trachea and bronchi carry air into the lungs; bronchioles are already inside them.

questions.explanation:
The answer is to transport air to the alveoli. Bronchioles are the small branching airways that carry air from the bronchi to the alveoli.

Blood vessels carry blood and nutrients, the alveoli exchange gases, and the trachea and bronchi carry air into the lungs.

Big idea: bronchioles are the last airways before the alveoli.

questions.prompt: The muscles surrounding the airways tighten and the airway lining becomes inflamed. The previous statement best describes:

choices.explanation: Correct. Tight airway muscles and inflamed lining describe asthma.
Incorrect. Emphysema destroys the alveoli.
Incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is caused by thick mucus from a gene defect.
Incorrect. Sleep apnea is pauses in breathing during sleep.

questions.explanation:
The answer is asthma. In asthma, the smooth muscle around the airways tightens (bronchoconstriction) and the airway lining becomes inflamed and swollen, often with extra mucus.

Emphysema destroys alveoli, cystic fibrosis is a genetic disease of thick mucus, and sleep apnea is pauses in breathing during sleep.

Big idea: asthma narrows the airways through muscle tightening and inflammation.

questions.prompt: The passive movement of oxygen down a concentration gradient

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Inspiration is breathing in.
Incorrect. Transpiration is water loss from plant leaves.
Incorrect. Convection is bulk movement of a fluid.
Correct. Diffusion moves oxygen down its concentration gradient.

questions.explanation:
The answer is diffusion. Diffusion is the passive movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration, without using energy.

Inspiration is breathing in, transpiration is water loss from plants, and convection is movement of a fluid carrying heat or substances.

Big idea: oxygen enters the blood by diffusion.

questions.prompt: The amount of air that moves in or out of the lungs with each respiratory cycle:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Eupnea is the name for normal breathing, not a volume.
Correct. Tidal volume is the air moved with each breath.
Incorrect. Respiratory rate is breaths per minute.
Incorrect. Residual volume stays in the lungs.

questions.explanation:
The answer is tidal volume, the amount of air moved in or out with each normal breath (about 500 mL).

Eupnea means normal quiet breathing, respiratory rate is breaths per minute, and residual volume is air that always stays in the lungs.

Big idea: tidal volume is one normal breath.

questions.prompt: What of the following is the correct path that oxygen takes when traveling to the lungs

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The larynx comes before the trachea.
Correct. Larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli.
Incorrect. The larynx comes first, and bronchi come before bronchioles.
Incorrect. Bronchi come before bronchioles.

questions.explanation:
The answer is larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli. After the nose and pharynx, air passes through the larynx (voice box), then the trachea (windpipe), then the bronchi, then smaller bronchioles, and finally the alveoli.

Big idea: the airway branches from large tubes to tiny air sacs.

questions.prompt: The tissue flap that closes when you swallow, keeping food and liquid out of the airway

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The mouth is where food enters.
Incorrect. The larynx is the opening being covered.
Correct. The epiglottis covers the airway during swallowing.
Incorrect. The trachea is the airway being protected.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the epiglottis, a flap of elastic cartilage above the larynx. When you swallow, it covers the larynx's opening so food and liquid go into the esophagus.

Big idea: the epiglottis keeps food out of the airway.

questions.prompt: During inspiration the diaphragm ______ and the thoracic cavity ______ in volume.

choices.explanation: Correct. The diaphragm contracts and the chest volume increases.
Incorrect. A contracting diaphragm makes the chest bigger.
Incorrect. The diaphragm contracts during inspiration.
Incorrect. This describes breathing out.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'contracts, increases'. When the diaphragm contracts, it flattens and moves down. This makes the thoracic (chest) cavity bigger, lowering pressure in the lungs so air flows in.

Big idea: the diaphragm contracts to breathe in.

questions.prompt: The following statements are all effects of high altitudes, EXCEPT:

choices.text: Lower oxygen saturation levels in blood
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Lower oxygen saturation does happen at high altitude.
Incorrect. Breathing can become unstable at high altitude.
Incorrect. Hyperventilation does happen at high altitude.
Correct. Heart rate increases, not decreases, at high altitude.

questions.explanation:
The answer is a decrease in heart rate. At high altitude, there is less oxygen, so heart rate goes UP, not down, to deliver oxygen faster.

The other effects do happen: oxygen saturation in the blood drops, breathing can become unstable (especially during sleep), and people breathe faster (hyperventilation).

Big idea: the body responds to low oxygen by working harder.

questions.prompt: All the following statements causes the oxygen dissociation curve to shift right, EXCEPT:

choices.explanation: Incorrect. High temperature shifts the curve right.
Incorrect. High acidity shifts the curve right.
Correct. High pH (less acid) shifts the curve left.
Incorrect. More CO2 shifts the curve right.

questions.explanation:
The answer is high pH. A right shift means hemoglobin releases oxygen more easily. High temperature, high acidity (low pH), and more CO2 all cause a right shift.

High pH means LESS acid, which shifts the curve to the left (hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly).

Big idea: heat, acid, and CO2 shift the curve right.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a membrane that protects and cushions the lungs

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The larynx is the voice box.
Incorrect. Capillaries are tiny blood vessels.
Correct. The pleura protects and cushions the lungs.
Incorrect. The trachea is the windpipe.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the pleura. The pleura is a two-layer membrane around each lung, with slippery fluid between the layers.

It protects the lungs and lets them slide smoothly against the chest wall. The larynx and trachea are airways, and capillaries are blood vessels.

Big idea: the pleura cushions and protects the lungs.

questions.prompt: What protects airways from harmful substances and irritants and filters the air that enters the body

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The epiglottis keeps food out of the airway.
Incorrect. Bronchioles carry air.
Correct. Cilia sweep trapped particles out of the airways.
Incorrect. The mouth is not the main air filter.

questions.explanation:
The answer is cilia. Cilia are tiny hairs on the airway lining. Together with mucus, they trap dust, germs, and irritants and sweep them up and out.

The epiglottis blocks food, bronchioles carry air, and the mouth is not the main filter.

Big idea: mucus and cilia clean the air you breathe.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are effects of exercise on the respiratory system

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but the others are true too.
Incorrect by itself. True, but the others are true too.
Incorrect by itself. True, but the others are true too.
Correct. Exercise causes all of these effects.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'All of the above'. Regular exercise improves circulation, strengthens the breathing muscles around the lungs, and increases the tidal volume (how much air you move per breath).

Big idea: exercise makes the respiratory system more efficient.

questions.prompt: What warms the air to match the body temperature and moisturizes it to the humidity level your body needs

choices.explanation: Correct. The sinuses and nasal cavity warm and moisten incoming air.
Incorrect. The trachea carries air; most warming has already happened.
Incorrect. The larynx is the voice box.
Incorrect. The epiglottis covers the airway during swallowing.

questions.explanation:
The key's answer is the sinuses. The paranasal sinuses (together with the nasal cavity) help warm and moisten the air you breathe in so it matches your body's temperature and humidity.

The trachea, larynx, and epiglottis are further down and do less of this conditioning.

Big idea: the upper airway prepares air before it reaches the lungs.

questions.prompt: The lower respiratory tract includes

choices.explanation: Incorrect. This leaves out the trachea and lungs.
Incorrect. This leaves out the trachea.

choices.text: Trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli
choices.explanation: Correct. The lower tract includes the trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli.

choices.text: Pharynx, trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The pharynx is part of the upper tract.

questions.explanation:
The answer is trachea, lungs, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli. The lower respiratory tract starts at the trachea and includes everything below it.

The pharynx belongs to the upper respiratory tract. Choices A and B leave out the trachea.

Big idea: upper tract = nose to pharynx; lower tract = trachea and below.

questions.prompt: Which part of the Respiratory System, known as the voice box, allows one to talk and make sounds when air moves in and out through the organ

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The mouth shapes sounds but does not produce them.
Correct. The larynx is the voice box.
Incorrect. The trachea carries air to the lungs.
Incorrect. The pharynx is the throat.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the larynx, the voice box. It contains the vocal cords, which vibrate as air passes through them to make sound.

Big idea: the larynx makes the voice.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure A.
questions.explanation:
Label A is the larynx (the epiglottis is also accepted). The line points to the boxy structure at the top of the windpipe in the neck.

The larynx holds the vocal cords and is covered by the epiglottis during swallowing.

Big idea: the larynx connects the pharynx to the trachea.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure B.
questions.explanation:
Label B is the trachea (windpipe), the tube running down the neck into the chest.

It is held open by C-shaped cartilage rings and carries air to the bronchi.

Big idea: the trachea is the main airway into the chest.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure C.
questions.explanation:
Label C is the bronchioles, the small branching airways inside the lungs.

They carry air from the bronchi to the alveoli.

Big idea: bronchioles connect bronchi to alveoli.

questions.prompt: Label the diagram: identify structure D.
questions.explanation:
Label D is the alveoli, shown as the cluster of tiny sacs in the box.

Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli.

Big idea: alveoli are where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

questions.prompt: Emphysema is a lung condition in which the alveoli inner walls rupture, creating bigger alveoli which reduces the surface area of the lungs. How does the reduced Surface area of the lungs affect gas exchange?

choices.explanation: Incorrect by itself. True, but C is also true.
Incorrect. Less surface area means less gas exchange.
Incorrect by itself. True, but A is also true.
Incorrect. Less oxygen reaches the blood.
Correct. Less gas exchange and less oxygen reaching the blood.
Incorrect. Gas exchange decreases, not increases.

questions.explanation:
The answer is 'Both A and C': less gas exchange happens, and less oxygen reaches the bloodstream. Gas exchange depends on surface area.

In emphysema, the walls between alveoli break down, leaving fewer, bigger air sacs with much less total surface. So less oxygen can diffuse into the blood.

Big idea: less surface area means less gas exchange.

questions.prompt: COPD is a chronic disorder in which the airways and alveoli in the lungs are unable to stretch and shrink back. How does their inability to stretch and shrink affect the gas exchange that occurs in the alveoli?
questions.answer: The lungs rely on the natural elasticity of the bronchial tubes and alveoli to force air in and out of the body. COPD causes them to lose their elasticity and over-expand, which leaves some air trapped in the lungs when exhaling. When waste like carbon dioxide get trapped in the lungs, less oxygen gets into body tissues, and it becomes harder to get rid of the waste gas carbon dioxide
questions.explanation:
The lungs rely on the natural stretchiness (elasticity) of the airways and alveoli to push air out. Normally, the stretched lungs spring back after each breath in, pushing air out.

In COPD, the lungs lose this elasticity and become over-expanded, so some air stays trapped when breathing out. Trapped, stale air keeps carbon dioxide in the lungs and leaves less room for fresh, oxygen-rich air, so less oxygen reaches the body and it is harder to get rid of carbon dioxide.

Big idea: elastic recoil is needed to empty the lungs; losing it traps air and impairs gas exchange.

questions.prompt: These are tiny sacs in the lungs through which the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place.

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Bronchi are airways that carry air into the lungs.
Incorrect. Breathing is a process, not a structure.
Correct. Alveoli are the tiny sacs where gas exchange happens.
Incorrect. Cilia are tiny hairs that sweep mucus out of the airways.

questions.explanation:
The answer is alveoli. Alveoli are tiny, balloon-like air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways. Their walls are only one cell thick and are wrapped in capillaries, so oxygen can move into the blood and carbon dioxide can move out.

Bronchi are tubes that carry air, breathing is the whole process of moving air, and cilia are tiny hairs that sweep mucus.

Big idea: gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is not part of the respiratory system?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. The trachea (windpipe) is a respiratory airway.
Incorrect. The pharynx carries air as well as food, so it is part of the respiratory system.
Correct. The esophagus carries food, so it is part of the digestive system.
Incorrect. A bronchus carries air into a lung.
Incorrect. The nasal cavity is where air first enters.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the esophagus. The esophagus is the food tube that carries swallowed food to the stomach, so it belongs to the digestive system.

The trachea, bronchus, and nasal cavity are all airways. The pharynx (throat) is shared by both systems, carrying both air and food.

Big idea: the trachea carries air; the esophagus behind it carries food.

questions.prompt: Which respiratory structure is used to produce sound?

choices.explanation: Correct. The larynx contains the vocal cords that make sound.
Incorrect. The nose changes how sound resonates but does not produce it.
Incorrect. The pharynx shapes sound but does not produce it.
Incorrect. The glottis is the gap between the vocal cords, only one part of the larynx.
Incorrect. The esophagus is a food tube.

questions.explanation:
The answer is the larynx, or voice box. It holds the vocal cords, which vibrate as air passes between them to make sound.

The glottis is just the opening between the vocal cords, part of the larynx. The nose and pharynx help shape the sound, and the esophagus carries food.

Big idea: the larynx produces the voice.

questions.prompt: What is the primary function of the bronchi?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. Most filtering happens in the nose and upper airways.

choices.text: Making the air colder and more humid
choices.explanation: Incorrect. The nose warms the air and makes it more humid; it does not cool it.

choices.text: Moving air from the trachea to the lungs
choices.explanation: Correct. Bronchi carry air from the trachea into the lungs.
Incorrect. The blood delivers oxygen to cells.

questions.explanation:
The answer is moving air from the trachea to the lungs. The trachea splits into two main bronchi, one for each lung, and they keep branching inside.

Filtering and moistening air happen mostly in the nose, and oxygen reaches cells through the blood.

Big idea: bronchi are the air pipes that connect the windpipe to each lung.

questions.prompt: What are the types of pulmonary ventilation?

choices.explanation: Incorrect. These are the everyday words; the scientific names are inspiration and expiration.
Incorrect. Panting is fast, shallow breathing, not a type of ventilation.
Correct. Inspiration and expiration are the two phases of ventilation.
Incorrect. These are not types of ventilation.

questions.explanation:
The answer is inspiration and expiration. Pulmonary ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs. Inspiration is the scientific name for breathing in, and expiration is breathing out.

'Inhaling and exhaling' means the same thing in everyday words, but this question wants the scientific names. Panting and 'full and new' are not the two types.

Big idea: ventilation has two phases, inspiration and expiration.

questions.prompt: What is the pleural membrane for?
